cues.text: You open a laptop, join a network, and ask for a web page. The server is several networks away. Nothing in between has ever heard of your laptop. So here is the question that drives this whole course. How does a packet reach the right place, when no single device knows the whole path?

The small network we will keep returning to. A laptop plugs into a switch on its own local network. A router called R1 connects that network to a middle network. A second router, R2, connects the middle network to the network where the web server lives. Three networks, two routers, and one packet to deliver.

The laptop builds a packet. Inside, in blue, is the IP header. Its destination is the server, 203.0.113.80. That address names the far end of the whole trip. But the wire can only carry the packet to a neighbor. So the laptop wraps it in a yellow Ethernet frame, which we will picture as an envelope, addressed to the only neighbor that can help, router R1.

Watch what each device actually reads. The switch reads only the yellow frame and passes it toward R1. It never looks at the blue address. R1 receives the frame, and its job with that envelope is finished.

The key moment comes. R1 tears off the yellow envelope, because that envelope only described one local hop. It reads the blue destination, chooses the next router, lowers the TTL from 64 to 63, and wraps the same blue packet in a brand new envelope. The yellow changed. The blue destination did not.

At R2 the same thing happens. Old envelope off, destination read, TTL down to 62, new envelope on, this time addressed to the server itself. The server is finally a direct neighbor, so the frame and the packet now point at the same machine.

Lay the whole trip out in one table, and the pattern is plain. The Ethernet addresses are different on every line. The IP endpoints are identical on every line. Only the TTL counts down, one for each router crossed.

The rule to carry through every chapter. A frame delivers across one link. A packet delivers across the whole network. Frames are replaced at each router. Packets keep their endpoints, unless something like a tunnel deliberately adds another layer, and we will meet that much later.
People say each router readdresses the packet to the next router. It doesn't. It replaces the frame, and the packet's source and destination stay fixed.

Change one fact. Suppose the destination is not far away. Suppose it is another machine on the laptop's own network, 192.0.2.53. The laptop's mask says this address is local. So what goes on the yellow envelope now?
Take a moment. Decide which address goes on the Ethernet frame, and whether any router gets involved.

The envelope is addressed directly to that machine, and R1 never sees the frame. The switch does all the delivery. Now the frame and the packet name the same destination from the very first hop. That choice, send directly or send to a router, is the first decision every host makes. The next dish names the layers that make this split possible, and every later chapter fills in one of the facts this little trip quietly assumed.

That trip involved a wire, a frame, a packet, and a web request. Why are these separate things at all? Why not design one giant protocol that does everything from pulling bits off a cable to fetching a page? The answer is that a problem this large has to be cut into pieces, and each piece must be able to change without breaking the others.

Networks are built as a stack of layers. The physical layer moves bits across a medium. The link layer moves a frame to a neighbor on that link. The network layer moves a packet across many links. The transport layer delivers data between programs on the two end machines. And the application layer is the program's own conversation, such as asking for a web page.

Each layer uses the service below it and offers a service to the one above. A protocol is an agreement between two parties at the same layer: what messages they send, in what format, and what they do when a message arrives. Because the agreement stays inside one layer, Ethernet can become Wi-Fi without anybody rewriting a web browser.

Going down the stack, each layer treats what it received as opaque data and wraps its own header around it. Going up on the far side, each layer removes its own header. That wrapping is called encapsulation, and it is exactly what you just watched. The yellow frame was the link layer's wrapper around the blue packet.

Connect this to delivery. Each wrapper has its own scope. Ethernet addresses mean something only on one local link. An IP address means something across the whole Internet, because every router understands how to move toward it. A transport port means something only inside the destination machine, selecting which program receives the data.

Every address answers a question at one particular scope. Who is my next neighbor? That is the link layer. Where is the final destination? That is the network layer. Mixing up those two questions causes most of the confusion in this course, so hold on to them.
A common slip is to treat a switch and a router as the same box. A switch forwards frames by MAC address, within one network. A router forwards packets by IP address, between networks.
Change the technology underneath. Replace the middle network, between R1 and R2, with a completely different kind of link, one that uses different frames and different local addresses.
Which headers have to change because of that swap, and which do not? Pick your answer before I continue.

Only the link header on that one hop changes. R1 builds whatever frame the new link needs. The IP header still names the same two endpoints, and the laptop and the server never find out. That is the payoff of layering. IP is the common layer that lets networks built from totally different hardware act as one Internet. With those pieces named, we can start at the bottom, with the first problem any local network faces: many machines, and one shared wire.

Our laptop's very first hop crosses a local network. So start there. Suppose many computers share one wire, and whatever one sends, everybody hears. If two speak at once, the signals garble each other. Who gets to talk, and when? Notice this is not a technical detail. It is a resource allocation problem.

One family of answers is channel partitioning. Divide the wire into fixed shares of time or frequency, one for each user. With four users on a 12 megabit per second wire, each user owns 3 megabits per second. It is perfectly fair and collision free. But watch what happens when only one user has anything to send. Three quarters of the wire sits idle, and that lone user still gets just 3.

A second family is taking turns. A controller polls each station, or a token passes around, so only the holder may send. Idle stations can be skipped, which fixes the waste. The price is control overhead, and a dependency on the coordinator or the token.

The third family is random access. Do not coordinate at all. Whoever has data just tries. When the network is quiet, a lone sender gets nearly the whole wire. When many are active, collisions waste capacity. None of the three wins everywhere. They make different trades among idle capacity, control overhead, and contention. Ethernet chose random access.

Before watching Ethernet contend, look at what it sends. A frame starts with a preamble, which lets the receiver's clock synchronize. Then a destination address, a source address, a type field saying what the payload is, such as IP, then the payload, and finally a CRC that detects corruption. The CRC only detects. It does not repair, and Ethernet sends no acknowledgment. Delivery here is best effort.

Those addresses are MAC addresses, 48 bits burned into each network interface. A MAC address is flat, like a serial number. It says nothing about location, and it has meaning only for local delivery. A network card keeps a frame only if the destination is its own address, or the broadcast address. Everything else, it ignores.

Picture one LAN. A host has one IP address and one MAC address, written as six hexadecimal bytes. A switch learns that MAC from incoming frames. A sending host learns the IP to MAC mapping through ARP. And the broadcast address is all ones.

The Ethernet rule, called CSMA/CD. Carrier sense: listen first, and if someone is talking, wait. Collision detection: keep listening while you send. If what you hear differs from what you sent, there is a collision, so stop and send a brief jam signal. But why would a collision ever happen, if everyone listens first? Because signals take time to travel. A and B can both hear silence, because neither signal has arrived yet.

After a collision, if both retry immediately, they collide again forever. So each picks a random wait. After the m-th collision, choose K from zero up to 2 to the m, minus one, and wait K times 512 bit times. Each further collision doubles the range, so the group spreads itself out without any coordination. That is binary exponential backoff. Try one. After the third collision, K ranges from 0 to 7. On 10 megabit Ethernet, 512 bit times is 51 point 2 microseconds. So K equal to 5 means a wait of 256 microseconds.

There is one more trap. A sender can only detect a collision while it is still transmitting. Suppose A starts at time zero, and the one-way delay is d. B starts just before A's signal arrives, at almost d. B's collision news then needs another d to return. So A may not hear about it until 2 d. So A must still be sending at 2 d, which gives the rule: frame length over rate must be at least twice the propagation delay.
A tempting one: if everyone listens before sending, collisions can't happen. But a signal takes time to travel, so two stations can both hear silence, and both start.

Put in the classic numbers. At 10 megabits per second, with a one-way delay of 25 point 6 microseconds, the frame must last at least 51 point 2 microseconds. That is 512 bits, which is the famous 64 byte minimum Ethernet frame. Now change the delay to just 20 microseconds, at the same rate.
What minimum length does the same formula give now, in bits?

Two times 20 microseconds times 10 megabits per second is 400 bits. That is the formula's answer. It does not replace Ethernet's real minimum of 64 bytes, and the rule belongs to shared, half-duplex wires. Notice what the whole design has been fighting: everyone shares one collision domain. So the next question is obvious. Could we simply stop sharing?
Plug eight machines into one box. Do they now have eight private conversations, or one big shared one? It depends entirely on what the box does with the bits.

A repeater amplifies a weakening signal, so a LAN can stretch further. A hub is a repeater with many ports. Every bit arriving on one port is copied out of all the others. It reads no addresses. It stores nothing. So a hub with eight ports is still one wire, wearing a different shape. If A sends to B while C sends to D, they collide. The boundary that matters is the collision domain, not the number of boxes in the picture.

Ethernet switching is different in kind. It receives a whole frame, reads the destination MAC address, and sends the frame only out the port that leads there. Now A to B and C to D run at the same time, through independent port pairs, with no collision at all. Each link has become its own little collision domain.

And with a private point to point link, a host can send and receive at once. That is a full-duplex link, and on it, collision detection has nothing left to do. Does that mean a switch never loses anything? No. If A and C both send to B, both frames need the same output. A switch has finite output rates and finite buffers, so frames must queue. We removed collisions, not contention.

One choice remains: when does the switch start sending? Store-and-forward switching receives the entire frame first, and checks the CRC, so bad frames die here. Cut-through switching begins as soon as it has read the destination address. That saves some waiting, but it may forward a frame that later turns out to be corrupt.

It helps to name exactly which delay is being removed. Reception time is frame length divided by rate. A 1500 byte frame at 100 megabits per second takes 120 microseconds just to arrive. Store-and-forward pays this at every switch.
People often say a switch fixes everything a hub got wrong. It doesn't stop broadcasts from spreading, and a collision-free output can still queue and drop.
Change the situation. Our frame's last bytes get corrupted on the way into the switch. And suppose the output port is busy, so the frame cannot begin leaving at once either.
Under cut-through, does the bad frame reach B? And what does cut-through save if the output was busy anyway?

With a free output, cut-through would already be sending when the corruption arrives, so a bad frame can reach B. With a busy output, the frame has to wait anyway, so the savings shrink. Store-and-forward would have discarded it. There is still a gap in the switch story. It sends a frame only out the right port. But how could a box you just took out of the packaging possibly know which port is right?

Nobody configures a home switch. You plug in the cables and it works. Yet it sends frames out the correct port. Where did that knowledge come from? Pause on a clue: every frame carries two addresses. Only one of them says where a machine actually is right now.

A switch with an empty table, and three hosts. A is on port 1, B is on port 2, and C is on port 3. A sends a frame to B. Watch the order of the next two steps, because they use two different addresses.

First, the switch looks at the source address. This frame says it came from A, and it arrived on port 1. So A must be reachable through port 1. Write that down. Second, it looks up the destination, B. B is not in the table, so the switch has no idea. It floods the frame out every other port. Note what it did not learn. It cannot learn where B is just because A mentioned B.

B answers. Its frame's source address teaches the switch that B is on port 2. And now the destination, A, is in the table, so this frame goes only out port 1. Finally, A sends to B once more. Nothing new to learn. The destination is known, and the frame goes only to port 2. C is no longer bothered.

The rule is, learn from the source, then forward by the destination. Unknown destination, flood. Known destination on another port, forward. Known destination on the arrival port, filter. Entries also expire, so that a host which moves or disappears does not stay wrong forever. The slides call this a TTL. Be careful with that word. It is a local aging timer in the switch. It is not a hop counter carried in the Ethernet frame, and that fact is about to matter a great deal.

Networks want spare links, in case one fails. So connect three switches in a triangle. Now send one broadcast. S1 floods it to S2 and S3. Each floods it onward, to the other. Those copies come back, and get flooded again. IP has a TTL that kills looping packets. Ethernet has no such field. The copies circulate and multiply until the network collapses. A cycle in the wiring is fatal.

The fix is the spanning tree protocol. Keep every physical link, but let frames use only a loop-free subset. Switches exchange messages carrying three things: who they think the root is, their distance to it, and their own ID. Each begins by claiming to be the root. Hearing a lower ID, it gives up that claim.

Hearing a shorter path to the root, it adopts that path. In the triangle, S1 becomes root, S2 and S3 use their direct links, and the link between them stops forwarding. Three switches, two active links, and no cycle. The slides simplify the real protocol, which also needs deterministic ties and a designated forwarder on each segment.

The exercise from the instructor's slides, with seven switches. The drawing gives no priorities or costs, so we must state an assumption. Treat all links as equal cost, and treat S1 through S7 as increasing bridge IDs. Then S1 is the root. Most switches connect to it directly. S3 is two hops away, through either S2 or S5, and the lower ID, S2, wins the tie. That leaves six active links for seven switches, exactly a tree.
Watch out for this one. When a switch floods an unknown destination, the frame doesn't become a broadcast. Its destination address stays exactly as it was. Only the set of output ports changed.
Use this tree. Host A hangs off S3, host B off S7, and host C off S4. A to B cannot use the short-looking route through S5, because those dashed links do not forward.
Trace the other two paths on the tree. What route does A to C follow? And B to C?

A to C goes S3, S2, S1, S4. B to C goes S7, S1, S4. Notice that A to B took three hops, though the physical drawing offers something shorter. Spanning tree does not promise shortest paths between hosts, and it does not minimize total cost either. It promises one thing: no loops. Different priorities could pick a different tree, so the assumptions stay attached to the answer.

A building has one set of switches, but two departments that should not share broadcasts. Finance sits on three different floors, mixed in with engineering. Do we have to rewire the building each time someone changes desks?

A virtual LAN lets one physical switching system act as several separate LANs. Group by organization rather than by location. A broadcast from a finance machine is now flooded only to finance ports, and engineering never sees it. A flood is confined to its VLAN, even though every frame crosses the same box.

How does a switch know which VLAN a frame belongs to? There are two ways. With port-based VLANs, membership belongs to the port. Ports 1 through 8 are VLAN 10, and ports 9 through 16 are VLAN 20. Whatever plugs into that port joins that VLAN. With MAC-based VLANs, membership follows the machine's address instead, so a laptop keeps its VLAN wherever it plugs in.

An independent-learning example. Ports 1 and 2 are VLAN 10. Ports 3 and 4 are VLAN 20. Port 5 is a trunk for both. Port 6 is in VLAN 10 but discards data. A frame from A enters port 1 for unknown B. Learn A in VLAN 10 on port 1. Flood only ports 2 and 5.

The same MAC, A, enters port 3 in VLAN 20. Learn a separate entry for A in VLAN 20 on port 3. B is unknown in this VLAN too, so flood only ports 4 and 5. The VLAN 10 entry is still there. This example uses independent learning, rather than claiming all hardware organizes its memory identically.
B replies on port 2 in VLAN 10. Learn B in VLAN 10 on port 2, then look up A within VLAN 10. The frame goes only to port 1. Neither the other VLAN nor the discarding port receives it.

Finally B replies on port 4 in VLAN 20. Learn B in VLAN 20 on port 4, then look up A within that VLAN. Send only to port 3. The VLAN context chooses which learned location is relevant. The trunk can carry both groups while keeping their identities separate.

Finance spans two switches, joined by one cable. That cable carries both departments. When a frame arrives at the far switch, how can it tell which VLAN the frame belongs to? The sending switch inserts a tag. This is 802.1Q trunking. It adds four bytes after the source address, including a 12 bit VLAN ID. Because the frame changed, the CRC is recomputed. The receiving switch reads the tag, and removes it before delivering to an ordinary host.

Before leaving the LAN, compare the three boxes we now have. A hub gives you no traffic isolation, and it needs no setup. A switch isolates traffic, and it's still plug and play, but flooding and spanning trees keep it from routing efficiently. An IP router isolates traffic and routes well, but it isn't plug and play, because someone must configure it. Each step up costs something, and buys something.

Keep the jobs separate. A VLAN decides who shares a broadcast domain. A trunk carries that identity between switches. Neither one moves traffic between different VLANs. For that, you need a router, even if the router lives inside a multilayer switch.
The slide's phrase can mislead you here. A trunk carries frames between switches, keeping their VLANs separate. It doesn't move traffic from one VLAN to another. That takes a router.
Change one thing. A finance laptop's owner moves desks, and plugs into a port in VLAN 20, the engineering VLAN, on a port-based switch.
Whose broadcasts does the laptop hear now? And can it keep its old IP address and still work?

It now hears engineering's broadcasts, because the port decided its membership. And if each VLAN is its own IP subnet, its old address no longer fits, so it needs a new configuration. The laptop is physically fine, yet logically it moved. Remember too that VLANs separate traffic, but they are no complete security proof. Addresses can be changed, and configuration decides what is accepted. That word, subnet, needs a real meaning. And it is the point where local delivery runs out. To go further, we need addresses with structure.

Our laptop's frame has reached the edge of its LAN. Beyond that lie thousands of networks, built by different owners, from different hardware. What should the network as a whole promise to deliver? A guaranteed rate? Guaranteed order? Or almost nothing at all? The surprising answer that built the Internet is: almost nothing.

One design comes from the telephone network: circuit switching. Before any data moves, set up a path, and reserve capacity at each hop. Once it is established, the bandwidth is yours. Quality is predictable. But if you pause, nobody else may use your reserved share, and every switch has to remember your call.

Put numbers on the waste. A 1 megabit per second circuit reserved for ten seconds allocates up to 10 megabits. If the application sends only 2, the rest of that opportunity can't necessarily be used by anyone else.

The other design is packet switching. Chop data into packets. Give each one its own destination address, and let each hop forward it when capacity becomes available. No setup, and no reservation. No router has to remember that you exist.

Why does this suit computers? Their traffic is bursty. A web page arrives in a rush, and then the link goes silent. Sharing capacity according to actual arrivals is called statistical multiplexing, and it lets many bursty users share a link that could never hold all their peaks. The price comes when bursts overlap. If 8 megabits per second arrive at a 4 megabit link for 10 milliseconds, a backlog of 5,000 bytes builds in a queue.

IP makes a modest deal called best-effort service. It will try. It may lose your packet, reorder it, delay it, or even duplicate it, and none of that breaks the contract. That sounds terrible, until you see what it buys. A network that promises so little can run over nearly any link, and needs no per-flow memory inside. Reliability can then be added at the end machines, by the programs that actually need it.

Best effort is not the only possible deal. A QoS service model is a list of promises about bandwidth, loss, order, and timing. ATM's constant bit rate service reserves a fixed rate, with order and timing protected. ATM's available bit rate promises only a minimum rate. Integrated Services aims at explicit guarantees per flow. Differentiated Services treats classes of packets differently, without per-flow guarantees. Keep these promises separate. A minimum rate is not a delay bound, and priority is not an end to end guarantee.

If routers remember nothing about flows, what do they keep? A forwarding table. And that exposes the most useful split in this course. The data plane handles every packet, using the installed table, in nanoseconds. The control plane exchanges information, and decides what belongs in that table, over seconds. The management plane is where people configure intent. Say an operator changes a link weight. A protocol recomputes. The router installs a new entry. Later packets follow it. Those are separate events, and that separation will matter when failures strike.

Traditionally, each router runs its own control software, and they cooperate. Software-defined networking moves that logic into a controller, which programs the forwarding devices. Does every packet then have to visit the controller? No. The controller installs rules, and the device applies them locally. Either way, the rule stays the same. Control decides. Data executes.
An easy mistake: if average load is below capacity, nothing should ever wait. But traffic comes in bursts, so queues still build for short moments.
Test yourself on the contract. A packet has a valid address. Its checksum is perfect, and a route exists. It still never arrives.
Did the network break its promise? Name two ways this could happen.

No promise was broken. A full queue may drop it. Its TTL may expire. A failure or a policy may stop it. Best effort means exactly that. So what does the network truly require from each packet? An address that can guide it across thousands of networks, without each router knowing every host. That is our next problem.

A switch can keep one table entry per machine, because a LAN is small. The Internet holds billions of interfaces. If every router needed an entry for every one, no router could cope. So how can a router in another country forward a packet toward your laptop without ever having heard of it?

An IPv4 address is simply a 32 bit number, written as four decimal bytes. Here is our example, 10.10.1.97. It identifies an interface, not a computer, so a router with three links has three addresses. And unlike a MAC address, this one has structure.

The structure is this. The leading bits name a network, and the trailing bits name a host within that network. The boundary is written after a slash. In 10.10.1.97/23, the first 23 bits are the network part, leaving 9 bits for hosts. A router far away only needs to know which way to send that whole block. Every host inside is covered by one entry. That is how the Internet scales.

Originally that boundary was forced. Classful addressing offered only three unicast sizes: slash 8, slash 16, and slash 24. An organization needing 300 addresses was too big for a slash 24, so it received a slash 16, with 65 thousand addresses, and wasted nearly all of them.

The class was even written into the address's first bits. An initial zero meant class A, one zero meant class B, and one one zero meant class C. Class D, beginning one one one zero, is multicast. Today the prefix is stated explicitly, so a first byte no longer implies a mask.

CIDR, classless inter-domain routing, lets the boundary fall anywhere. Now the 300 address organization takes a slash 23, with 512 addresses. Each bit you add to the prefix halves the block. A slash 24 has 2 to the 8th, which is 256. A slash 23 has twice that. CIDR also allows aggregation. Two halves of one slash 24 can be announced as that single slash 24. But two ranges that merely look close may not combine, because a block must be aligned on its own size.

Who hands out these blocks? Allocation is hierarchical too. ICANN allocates to regional registries. Those allocate to Internet providers and large institutions, who pass smaller blocks on to their customers. So 12.0.0.0/8 might contain 12.3.0.0/16, which contains 12.3.1.0/24. A provider can then announce one short prefix for all of its customers together. The address hierarchy mirrors the business hierarchy, and it's what keeps routing tables manageable. Compare that to a switch, whose table lists individual machines.

To compute with a prefix, write it as a subnet mask. That is 32 bits with ones over the network part, and zeros over the host part. A slash 23 is 255.255.254.0. Now apply it. A bitwise AND of address and mask keeps the network bits, and clears the host bits. The result is the network address, 10.10.0.0. Notice what happened in the third byte. The 1 was cleared, because that last bit belongs to the host part.

Do the opposite. Set every host bit to one, and you get the broadcast address of this subnet, 10.10.1.255. The all zeros and all ones host patterns are reserved. So this block has 512 addresses in total, and 510 usable ones, from 10.10.0.1 through 10.10.1.254.

That subtraction of two applies to ordinary subnets. A slash 31 point to point link and a slash 32 host route need their own interpretation, so do not apply it blindly. The real rule is this. An address alone tells you nothing about its subnet. You need the mask.
A tempting shortcut is to compare the first three bytes of two addresses. That only works for a slash 24. For any other prefix, apply the actual mask.
A trap on purpose. In this same slash 23, consider the address 10.10.0.255. It ends in 255.
Is it a broadcast address? Look at the host bits, not at the decimal number.

No. Its host part is 0 11111111, and that first zero means the bits are not all ones. It is an ordinary host address, sitting in the middle of the block. The ending 255 only signals broadcast when the mask says the last byte alone is the host part. So the numbers are only half of the picture, and the other half is the header that carries them. Let us open that up.

What does a router actually need to read? The IPv4 header has only about a dozen fields, and each exists to solve one bounded problem. Read them by purpose and by unit, because the units are where the traps are.

The header. Version says 4. IHL, the header length, counts 32 bit words, not bytes. So a value of 5 means 20 bytes. A packet with IHL 6 and total length 1024 therefore has 24 header bytes, and 1000 bytes of payload.

Total length counts the whole datagram in bytes, and it is a 16 bit field. So the largest value is 2 to the 16th, minus one, which is 65,535 bytes. The slide prints 63,535. That is a typo, and the arithmetic settles it.

The protocol field names what comes next, such as TCP, 6, or UDP, 17. It is not a port number. Follow the chain of hand-offs. Ethernet's type says this payload is IPv4. IPv4's protocol says this payload is UDP. UDP's destination port selects the program.

TTL limits the damage from routing loops. Every router lowers it by one, and at zero the packet dies, and the router normally sends back an ICMP time exceeded message. A clever tool turns this into a map. Traceroute sends a probe with TTL 1. The first router replies. Then TTL 2, and the second router replies. Each reply reveals one more hop. A missing reply may just mean a router declines to answer.

One more field is linked to TTL. The header checksum is a one's complement sum over the header only. It does not cover the payload, it does not authenticate anybody, and it cannot repair errors. And here is the consequence. Each router lowers the TTL, which changes the header. So each router must also update the checksum. With TTL 64, our example header's checksum works out to one value. With TTL 63, it is a different one.
Read each field with its unit. IHL is in 32 bit words. Total length is in bytes. Fragment offset is in 8 byte units. TTL is in router hops. Mixing these up is how most header questions are lost.
A common overclaim. The IPv4 checksum doesn't protect the payload, doesn't correct anything, and doesn't authenticate a sender. It only detects errors in the header.
A new situation. A forwarding loop forms between R1 and R2, and a packet enters it with TTL 64. Meanwhile a DNS answer has a TTL of 300, and our switch table has a timer too.
Does TTL rescue this packet? And do those three things called TTL all count the same thing?

TTL does not rescue it. It only ends it, after using up link capacity, so the damage is bounded rather than prevented. And the three are different. IP's TTL counts router hops. A DNS TTL counts seconds of cache life. A switch table timer ages an entry locally. Same acronym, different arithmetic. One field group remains, those fragmentation fields, so let us use them.
IP runs over any link, and links limit how big a packet they will carry. That limit is the MTU. What happens when a 4,000 byte datagram reaches a link with an MTU of only 1,500 bytes?

If fragmentation is allowed, the router splits it into smaller datagrams. Each fragment gets its own full IP header, so each travels independently. They all keep the original's identification number, so the destination can tell which ones belong together. Reassembly normally happens only at the destination.

The arithmetic, carefully. Total length is 4,000, and 20 bytes of that is header. So the data to carry is 3,980 bytes. Each fragment on the small link can hold 1,500 minus 20, which is 1,480 bytes of data. And nonfinal fragments must carry a multiple of 8 bytes, because the offset field counts in 8 byte units. 1,480 divides evenly by 8. So 1,480 it is.

The first fragment carries bytes 0 through 1,479, offset 0, more fragments flag set. The second carries the next 1,480. Its offset is 1,480 divided by 8, which is 185. The flag is still set. The third carries what remains, 1,020 bytes. Its offset is 2,960 divided by 8, which is 370, and its more fragments flag is 0, marking the end.

Check it. The payloads sum to 3,980, which is the original data, restored exactly. But the total bytes sent are 4,040, not 4,000, because there are now three headers instead of one. Fragmentation costs overhead, and if any one fragment is lost, the whole datagram is lost.

Keep the rule short. Offset is the data position in the original, divided by 8. It is not the fragment's length, and it does not count headers. Fragmentation exists to fit a link, and it has nothing to do with repairing congestion loss.
One more trap. A router can't always fragment. If the Don't Fragment flag is set, it isn't allowed to. And losing any one fragment loses the whole datagram.
New numbers. Total length 3,200, header 20, MTU 1,000. This time 1,000 minus 20 is 980, and 980 is not a multiple of 8.
What is the largest nonfinal payload? How many fragments will there be, and what are their offsets?

Round 980 down to a multiple of 8, and you get 976. The data is 3,180 bytes, giving payloads of 976, 976, 976, and a final 252. The offsets go up in steps of 122: 0, 122, 244, 366. Those four unused bytes per fragment are the price of 8 byte alignment. We now know what a packet looks like. Next question: how does an organization carve up its address space, and how does a router pick among overlapping routes?

Our laptop's network got its addresses from somewhere. An organization holds one block, and four departments of very different sizes. How do you cut the block so that everyone fits, nothing overlaps, and routers can still describe each piece with a single prefix?

Start with size, not with addresses. A subnet with h host bits holds 2 to the h addresses. Two are reserved, for the network and the broadcast. So to hold H hosts, choose the smallest h where 2 to the h, minus 2, is at least H. The prefix length is then 32 minus h. Using different sizes inside one block is called variable length subnet masking.

To feel the trade, take one slash 24 and start borrowing host bits for subnets. Borrow 1 bit: 2 subnets, with 7 host bits left, so 126 hosts in each. Borrow 2 bits: 4 subnets of 62 hosts. Borrow 3: 8 subnets of 30. Each borrowed bit doubles the number of subnets, and roughly halves their size. Keep going, and at 7 borrowed bits, only one host bit remains. The formula then gives zero ordinary hosts. A slash 31 needs its own point to point interpretation, so don't apply the subtraction blindly there.

Why does a host care about all this? Because the mask is how it makes its first decision. Before sending, it ANDs the destination with its own mask, and compares that with its own network. If they match, the destination is on this link, so it sends directly. If not, it sends to its gateway. Routers apply masks too, but to a whole table of prefixes, as we'll see in a moment.

The instructor's example. Four departments need 130, 120, 60, and 31 hosts, inside a slash 23. The slide labels the parent 128.101.5.0/23. Apply the mask, though. A slash 23 forces the last bit of the third byte to zero, and 5 is odd. So the true network is 128.101.4.0/23. It covers third byte values 4 and 5, and the slide's department blocks fit this normalized parent.

Allocate the largest first, since that keeps the blocks aligned. Department A needs 130. 7 host bits give only 126, so it takes 8 bits, a slash 24, the first half of the parent. B needs 120, and 7 bits give 126. That is a slash 25, at 128.101.5.0. C needs 60. 6 bits give 62, so a slash 26. D needs 31. It is tempting to pick a slash 27, because 32 addresses seem like enough. But a slash 27 leaves only 30 usable. So D also needs a slash 26.

See the blocks laid along the parent. 256 plus 128 plus 64 plus 64 is 512, and that fills the slash 23 exactly. Each block begins on a multiple of its own size, which is what lets a single prefix describe it.
Check any allocation three separate ways. Does each subnet have enough usable hosts? Do any overlap? And is each one contained in the parent? A plausible looking dotted address proves none of those.
The mistake that looks harmless: placing a block wherever there's room. A block must begin on a multiple of its own size. Otherwise, no single prefix can describe it.
Change one requirement. Department C's count of 60 did not include its router interface or its printers. The real requirement is 63 interfaces.
What prefix does C need now? And does the whole plan still fit in the slash 23?

6 bits give only 62 usable, so C jumps to 7 bits, a slash 25, with 128 addresses. Add that up: 256, plus 128, plus 128, plus 64, is 576. That is more than 512, so the plan no longer fits. A single extra host at a boundary doubled the block, which is why you must state exactly what the count includes. The result is a table of overlapping prefixes on every router, so how does a router choose among them?

R1 holds a table of prefixes. Because prefixes can nest, one destination can match several entries at once. Which one should win? And how can a router decide this in a few nanoseconds, a few million times every second?

A router's table with three entries. 201.10.0.0/21 goes out output A. Inside that block, 201.10.6.0/23 goes out output B. And 0.0.0.0/0 goes out output C. Those entries overlap on purpose. The slash 21 is an aggregate, the slash 23 is an exception carved out of it, and the slash 0 is the fallback.

A packet arrives for 201.10.6.17. To test a route, mask the destination with the route's prefix length and compare. Under the slash 21 mask it matches. Under the slash 23 it also matches. And slash 0 matches everything. Three matches. The rule is longest prefix match. Choose the match with the most network bits, because it is the most specific claim. So the slash 23 wins, and the packet leaves on output B.

201.10.4.8. Its third byte, 4, lies within the slash 21, which covers 0 through 7, but not within the slash 23, which covers only 6 and 7. So output A. And 203.0.113.8 matches only the fallback, so output C. A route's position in the list does not matter. Neither does any metric from an unrelated route. Only prefix length decides among installed matches.

Let's see this at the level of bits, because that's what the hardware does. Write the destination, 201.10.6.17, above the route's network, 201.10.6.0. Under a slash 23, only the first 23 bits count. Compare them. Every one matches, so this route matches. Whatever's to the right of the boundary doesn't matter. Now compare 201.10.4.8 against that same route. Look at the third byte. 4 is 00000100, and 6 is 00000110. They differ in bit 23, inside the prefix. So that's no match, and that second packet falls through to the shorter route.

The speed problem. Scanning every route is far too slow. On a 10 gigabit link with 64 byte packets, there are about 19 and a half million packets each second, which leaves 51 point 2 nanoseconds per packet. That calculation leaves out Ethernet's physical overhead, so treat it as a budget illustration. But the conclusion holds. There is no time for a linear scan.

One answer is a trie, a tree you walk one address bit at a time. Follow the destination's bits down from the root. Whenever you pass a node holding a route, remember it. If the path dead-ends deeper down, you still have the last route you remembered. That is why a failed deep branch does not lose the earlier match. A Patricia trie compresses long chains with no branching, and multi-bit nodes trade memory for fewer steps.

The other answer is hardware. Ordinary memory takes an address and returns the content. Content-addressable memory does the reverse. Give it a key, and it compares against every entry at the same time. A plain CAM needs exact matches, which suits MAC tables. Prefixes have don't care bits. TCAM adds a third state, so a stored entry can say these bits must match, and these do not matter. Several entries can still match, so hardware priority must favor the longest prefix.

Once you can match bit patterns, why stop at the destination? Generalized forwarding matches on selected header fields and applies a configured action, such as forward, drop, or rewrite. That connects back to software-defined networking. Whether by prefix or by general match, the principle holds. Control installs the rules. The data plane applies them, one packet at a time.
The classic slip is stopping at the first match, or taking the lowest cost. In a table, order doesn't matter. In a trie, you keep walking, and remember the longest valid prefix so far.
Add a route. An operator installs 201.10.6.16/28 going to a new output, D, and a metric says the slash 21 is an excellent path. Our first packet, 201.10.6.17, comes back through.
Which output does it take now? And what would 201.10.6.33 do?

The slash 28 covers 201.10.6.16 through 31, so 201.10.6.17 goes to D. The metric never entered into it. And 201.10.6.33 is outside the slash 28, so the slash 23 catches it, output B. Finding the output is only half of forwarding, though. The packet still has to physically cross the router. So let us go inside.

A router has found the right output. Now a packet must physically cross the machine, while packets arrive on every other port too. Where can this go wrong? When a router is slow, which part is actually the bottleneck?

A router has four main parts. Input ports receive the bits, check the link layer, and do the lookup. A switching fabric moves packets between ports. Output ports buffer and transmit them. And a routing processor runs the control plane, computing the tables that input ports use. Follow our packet: in, lookup, across, queue, out.

The fabric's capacity is the first limit. With 4 inputs, each at 10 gigabits per second, up to 40 gigabits per second may be offered. A fabric that cannot move that much makes inputs wait, even when every output is free. There are three classic designs.
The oldest design is memory switching. The packet is copied into shared memory, and then copied out again. Each packet crosses memory twice, so memory bandwidth must be double the useful throughput.

Put a number on it. If a memory system can sustain 20 gigabits per second of copying, each forwarded bit is copied twice, so the router tops out near 10 gigabits per second, before any other overhead.

Next is a shared bus. A packet crosses directly from input to output, over one internal bus. That avoids the double copy. But only one packet can use the bus at a time, so the bus speed caps the entire router.

Again, a number. Four 10 gigabit inputs feed a 20 gigabit bus. They offer 40 gigabits per second, and only 20 can cross, even if every output link sits idle. The bus is the bottleneck, before the outputs are even considered.

The third design is an interconnection network, such as a crossbar. Now input 1 to output 2 and input 2 to output 1 can transfer at the same moment, over separate crossing points. Clos networks build big fabrics out of small switching stages. Many of them chop packets into fixed internal cells. Those cells are an internal technique, not IP fragments.

There's still a limit. Input 1 to output 2 and input 2 to output 1 can move together. But send both inputs to output 1, and they contend for that one output. Parallel paths inside the fabric create no extra capacity at a single output.

Even a crossbar has a trap. If two inputs want the same output at once, one must wait. Say input B and input C both have a head packet for output 1. B wins. C's head packet stays blocked. Now look behind it. C's second packet wants output 2, and output 2 is idle. But the queue is first in, first out, so that packet is stuck behind the blocked head. This is head of line blocking. A free output sits unused because of how the queue is arranged.

Packets can also wait at the output, and this limit is physical. Three 1,500 byte packets arrive together at a 12 megabit per second output. Each needs 1 millisecond to transmit. So they finish at 1, 2, and 3 milliseconds, after waiting 0, 1, and 2. A faster fabric can't help, because the wire has a fixed rate. If arrivals keep exceeding that rate, the buffer eventually fills, and something is dropped. A drop policy chooses what to discard. A scheduler chooses what to send next. Priority shifts who suffers, but it creates no new bits per second.

Step back from the queues, and look at the timescales in this machine. The data plane forwards, buffers, and schedules, in nanoseconds per packet, in line card hardware. The control plane runs routing and signaling, in tens of milliseconds to seconds per event, in router software. The management plane is people and scripts doing analysis and configuration, in minutes to hours. Tables could be typed in statically, but static entries don't adapt to failures, new equipment, or load.

It's also a good moment to compare our two forwarding worlds, as the instructor's questions do. Are both MAC and IP addresses allocated hierarchically? Yes, both are: MAC blocks go to vendors, and IP blocks go down through registries. Which is organized by topology? Only IP. Which forwards by exact match? MAC, since IP uses longest prefix. Which builds its table automatically, by watching data? Ethernet switches. Which keeps per-host state in the network? MAC. Routers keep state per prefix. And which keeps per-connection state? Neither one. These answers are worked out from the lecture's material, as the slide gives no key.
Before proposing a fix, find the contention. Is it at lookup, in the memory or bus or fabric, in an input queue, or at the output? Upgrading one simply moves the bottleneck to another.
Careful with memory switching. Its internal copy rate is not its useful throughput. Each packet crosses memory twice, so useful throughput is half.
Picture this. Ten senders all saturate one 10 gigabit output. Somebody proposes doubling the fabric speed.
Will it help? What would a bigger buffer do instead?

It won't. Packets just reach the same full output sooner. A bigger buffer absorbs short bursts, but under persistent overload it only adds delay before the same drops. The output's rate is the limit. That finishes the forwarding path, given a table. We assumed our laptop already knew its own address, its router, and its destination. It knew none of them when it woke up. So how does it find out?

Rewind to the moment the laptop wakes up. It holds one thing: its burned-in MAC address. It has no IP address, no mask, no idea where the router is, and no way to translate a name like www.example.test. How does it get from knowing nothing to sending a packet?

It needs three kinds of identifier, because they answer three different questions. A name is for people, and it can stay the same when a service moves. An IP address says where an interface sits in the topology. A MAC address gets a frame across one local link. Each translation between them is a separate protocol. That indirection is what lets a server change its address while its name stays fixed.

The habit to build. Before naming a protocol, state the missing fact. I need my own address and my gateway: that is DHCP. I need the MAC address of my next hop: that is ARP. I need the IP address behind a name: that is DNS.

Start with the bootstrap problem. The laptop needs to ask a server for an address. But it has no address to send from, and it doesn't know where any server is. There is a way out of that circle. Local broadcast reaches everyone on the LAN, with no configuration at all. So DHCP begins with a shout.

Four messages follow. Discover: is any DHCP server out there? Offer: a server proposes an address, say 192.0.2.10, along with a mask, a gateway, a DNS resolver, and a lease time. Several servers might offer. Request: the client announces which offer it chooses. ACK: that server confirms. Only after the ACK does the client begin using the address. An offer alone is just a proposal.

Look at what the laptop now knows. Its address, 192.0.2.10, with a slash 24 mask. Its gateway, 192.0.2.1. Its resolver, 198.51.100.53. It knows what counts as local, and where to send everything else. Yet it still does not know the gateway's MAC address. Knowledge arrives in stages, not in one magic connected moment.

Why does the address come with a lease? Suppose a laptop crashes, or simply leaves. It never says goodbye. If allocations were permanent, the pool would slowly drain. With a lease, the allocation expires unless it is renewed. This is called soft state: information that disappears on its own unless refreshed. Failed machines clean up after themselves, by doing nothing. A reservation is different. An administrator configures a fixed address for a particular machine, and the server hands it out centrally each time.

The laptop wants to send through its gateway, 192.0.2.1. A frame needs a MAC address, and it has only an IP address. So it checks its ARP cache. Empty. It broadcasts: who has 192.0.2.1? Every machine on the LAN hears. Only R1 replies, directly: that's me, and here is my MAC. The laptop caches that mapping for a while. Another soft state table.

ARP resolves only the next local hop, never the whole path. And don't confuse it with the switch's table. The host's ARP table maps IP to MAC. The switch's table maps MAC to port. Both changed during that exchange, and neither replaces the other. The rule is: route first, resolve the next hop's MAC second, transmit third.
Keep these lookups apart. ARP doesn't resolve a hostname, and DNS doesn't choose the Ethernet destination. DNS maps a name to an IP. ARP maps an IP to a MAC.
Change the target. The laptop now wants to send to the DNS resolver, 198.51.100.53. Apply the slash 24 mask to both addresses. 192.0.2.0 is not 198.51.100.0.
Which IP address does the laptop put in its ARP request?

It asks for the gateway, 192.0.2.1, never for the resolver, because ARP cannot cross a router. If the resolver were on the same subnet, at 192.0.2.53, it would ARP for the resolver directly. So the mask chooses the next hop, and the next hop chooses the ARP target. The laptop can now reach its resolver. But what does a resolver actually do? How can any system answer for every name on Earth?

The browser has the name www.example.test. It needs an address. There are billions of names, changing constantly, owned by millions of organizations. Could one file hold them? Could one giant server answer them all?

The two obvious designs fail. A hosts file downloaded by everyone would be enormous, and always stale. One central server would be a single point of failure, a traffic bottleneck, and far away from most people. So DNS distributes the database, by splitting up responsibility.

Names form a tree, read from the right. The root delegates to top-level domain servers, such as dot test or dot com. Those delegate to authoritative servers for each organization's zone. A zone is a piece of the tree under one administration. Nobody holds everything. Each server only knows who to ask next. By the way, you may hear about 13 root servers. That is 13 named identities, A through M, each deployed as many physical instances around the world.

Follow one lookup with empty caches. The laptop asks its resolver: please find this name for me. That is a recursive query. It asks the server to do all the work. The resolver then asks the root. The root doesn't know the answer, but it gives a referral: ask the dot test servers. The resolver asks those, and gets another referral: ask example dot test. It asks that authoritative server, and gets the answer. Those are iterative queries. Each returns an answer or a pointer, and leaves the next step to the asker. The result returns to the laptop: 203.0.113.80.
One lookup uses both styles. The client to resolver request is recursive. The resolver's walk down the tree is iterative. An exam question that asks which one DNS uses is really asking, which hop?

Doing all that for every request would crush the root. So the resolver caches. Each answer carries a TTL, in seconds. Store a record with TTL 300 at noon, and it can be reused until 12:05. Now the catch. If the real address changes at 12:01, the cache keeps giving out the old one for four more minutes. A shorter TTL narrows that window, at the cost of more lookups. That's a straight trade between freshness and load. Resolvers also cache referrals, so most queries never touch the root.

Resolvers remember failures too. Negative caching stores the answer that a name doesn't exist. Repeated typos, like www dot example dot tesst, then fail quickly, instead of walking the tree each time. There's a downside. A brand new name might stay hidden behind an unexpired negative answer. And don't confuse a genuine no such name result with a mere timeout.

Imagine someone keeps typing a name with a letter missing. Once the resolver learns that name doesn't exist, it can fail those requests quickly, until the negative result expires. A timeout is different. It only means no answer arrived, not that the name is missing.
Same word, different meaning. A DNS TTL is a cache lifetime, in seconds. An IP TTL is a hop limit. And a switch's aging timer is different again.
Change the state of the cache. A second laptop on the same LAN asks for www.example.test 4 minutes after the first one. The resolver stored the record with TTL 300.
How many queries does the resolver send to the hierarchy? And what about a third laptop at 5 minutes exactly?

At 240 seconds the cache is still valid, so zero queries leave the resolver. At 300 seconds the entry has expired, so it must ask again, though a cached referral could skip the root. Caching removes hierarchy traffic only. The packets to the web server still need routes and frames. Next, let us see what else this database holds.

A DNS answer isn't just a name and an address. How does the same system tell you where to send email, or which server is in charge of a zone? And what happens if the question or its answer simply gets lost?

DNS stores typed resource records, each with a name, a type, a value, and a TTL. An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address. An NS record names the server authoritative for a zone. A CNAME maps an alias to its canonical name. An MX record names a domain's mail exchanger, with a preference. Notice that NS, CNAME, and MX values are hostnames, not addresses. So they may need another lookup, to find an address.

DNS usually runs over UDP, which recovers nothing. So reliability is built above it. Zones keep replicated servers. Clients use timeouts, retry, and try a different server. Replies are matched to questions by an ID. DNS can also use TCP, so UDP is common, not exclusive.

Walk through a failure. A resolver queries server A, and hears nothing. After its timer, it tries replica B, and it accepts a reply only if it matches the outstanding request. Repeating immediately to the same failed server would add load, without helping.

We can tell the whole story in order, and there's a surprise in it. To reach the name, the laptop must query the resolver. But the resolver is remote. So before the DNS query can even leave, the laptop must ARP for its gateway. Then the frame goes to R1, carrying a packet to the resolver. The DNS answer returns. Only then can it send to the server, and a TCP connection can begin. The recap slide compresses that handshake. The classic form ends with a final ACK after the SYN and SYN-ACK.

How does a new name enter this system? Say a startup called FooBar registers foobar.com. The registrar inserts two records into the dot com servers: an NS record saying that foobar.com is served by dns1.foobar.com, and an A record giving that server's address. That second one is needed, because otherwise you'd have to resolve dns1.foobar.com in order to reach the server that answers for foobar.com. On its own server, FooBar then adds an A record for www, and an MX record for mail.

You can watch all of this with a tool called dig. A plain query prints three sections. The answer section has the record you asked for. The authority section names the servers responsible for that zone. The additional section gives those servers' addresses, which saves another lookup. An address shown under additional isn't necessarily the web server you asked about. Running dig with plus trace shows the entire walk from root to TLD to authoritative. And asking a TLD server directly, with recursion off, returns no answer at all, only a referral. That's an iterative reply, visible in plain text.

The instructor's slides run this as a compact example: host A, router R, host B. A's address is 111.111.111.111, and B's is 222.222.222.222. A's mask says that B is off-subnet, so A uses ARP to learn R's near-side MAC. The frame runs from A's MAC to R's MAC, while the IP header reads A to B.

R removes the frame, looks up B's prefix, finds B's MAC on the outgoing subnet, and emits a new frame from its far-side MAC to B's MAC. There it is again: the Ethernet destination is R on one link, and B on the other. The IP endpoints never change, in this ordinary trace with no NAT.

There's no fixed order that says DNS comes before ARP. What is missing right now decides what happens next. The name's address is missing, so we need DNS. To reach DNS, we need the gateway's MAC, so we need ARP first. Discovery traffic has its own delivery dependencies.
A frequent confusion. A CNAME is not an HTTP redirect. It's an alias inside DNS, so the resolver just looks up another name. The browser never gets sent to a new URL.
Change three facts. Put the resolver on the laptop's own subnet. Make the DNS answer already cached. And then cut the link between R1 and R2.
For each change, which steps disappear, and which still have to happen?

A local resolver means the laptop ARPs for the resolver directly. A cached answer removes the hierarchy queries, but the web packet still needs its gateway and its routes. And a cut link? All of the laptop's DNS and ARP entries remain perfectly correct, yet delivery still fails, because R1's forwarding table is now wrong or incomplete. That table is the one piece we've taken for granted since the start. Who fills it in? That is routing.

We ended the last chapter with a cut link, and a router whose table had gone wrong. So who fills in that table? A router forwards a packet using a table it reads in nanoseconds. But something has to build that table, and rebuild it when the network changes. An administrator cannot type routes into thousands of routers by hand. So how can routers, talking only to each other, work out good paths through a network none of them can see all at once?
Remember our laptop's packet, sitting at router R1, headed for a web server. R1 looked up the destination, and sent it out one port. This chapter is about where that table entry came from.

Start by separating two words. Forwarding is what a router does to one packet, right now: read the address, look it up, and send it out. Routing is how the table got there in the first place, a network-wide process of exchanging information and computing paths. And a route to a far prefix needs two pieces of knowledge. Which router, or exit, can reach that prefix? And how do I reach that router from here? This lecture solves the second piece. BGP will supply the first. Could you just type all this in by hand? Static routes don't adapt to failures, new equipment, or load.

First we need a model. Draw the network as a graph, with routers as nodes and links as edges, each with a cost. A path's cost is the sum of its edge costs. Our goal is the cheapest path from a source to each destination. If every edge costs one, this just counts hops.

But weights change the answer. Here, going from A to C directly costs 5. Going through B costs 2 plus 1, which is only 3. So the path with more hops is the better one. This makes sense inside one organization, where everyone agrees what the numbers mean. We'll see later that it does not fit the whole Internet.

One approach is link-state routing, and its idea has two steps. Step one: every router tells everyone about its own links. Those messages flood through the whole network, so eventually every router holds the same map. Step two: each router independently runs a shortest path computation on its copy of that map, with itself as the source. It shares facts, not conclusions. OSPF and IS-IS are the two link-state protocols you will meet in practice, both used inside a single organization.

One caution about that shared map. It's what the router currently believes, not a perfect live view of the network. If a link has just failed, some routers don't know yet. Hold on to that thought, because it creates a whole chapter of trouble. For now, assume every router's map is correct, and look at the computation itself, which comes from Edsger Dijkstra.

Dijkstra's algorithm grows a region of settled nodes, whose best distances are final. It keeps a tentative distance for every other node. Then it repeats one step. Pick the unsettled node with the smallest tentative distance, and settle it. Next, relax its edges: for each neighbor v, ask whether going through this node beats the best distance we had. Why is it safe to settle that smallest node? Because weights are not negative, so any other route to it would have to leave through a node that is already at least as far. No detour could ever come back cheaper.
Run it from A. Start by settling A, at distance zero. Its neighbors get tentative distances equal to their direct costs: B is 2, and C is 5. D is not adjacent, so D is infinity.

The frontier holds B at 2, C at 5, and D at infinity. The smallest is B, so settle it, and record that its predecessor is A. Relax B's edges. Through B, C costs 2 plus 1, which is 3. That beats 5, so C improves, and its predecessor becomes B. Through B, D costs 2 plus 4, which is 6, and that beats infinity.

The frontier is C at 3, and D at 6. Settle C, through B. Relax its edge to D: 3 plus 2 is 5. That beats 6, so D improves again, and its predecessor changes from B to C. See how a tentative value can keep getting better until the moment it's settled, and never after that.
Finally settle D, at 5, through C. Every node is settled. The green edges form a shortest path tree, rooted at A. Final distances: B is 2, C is 3, and D is 5.

The part that catches people out. The computation gave us predecessors, but a forwarding table needs something else. D's predecessor is C. That is the node just before D on the path. But router A cannot hand a packet to C. It is not even the right neighbor. The path to D is A, B, C, D, so A's forwarding entry says: to reach D, send to B. In fact, every entry at A says B here. Distance, predecessor, and first hop are three different outputs. The first hop is the only one a forwarding table stores.

Try the instructor's exercise. On this graph, find the shortest path from t to v. It's tempting to go through x, since t reaches x directly at 5. But then x to z to y to v adds 3, for a total of 8. The direct route from x to v, at 4, also gives a total of 8 by way of s and w. The best path is t, s, w, x, z, y, v, adding 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, and 1, which is 7. So the distance is 7, answer B, and the forwarding entry at t points to s, also answer B. More hops, lower cost.

The slides also trace a bigger graph from source A, over eight nodes. The method doesn't change. Settle B at 2, which improves D from 5 to 4, and gives E 9 and F 14. C and D then tie at 4. Either may go first, since a tie can alter a predecessor but no shortest distance.

Settling D improves E to 8, and gives G 7. Settling G offers E another route costing 8, another tie. Settling E improves H from 14 to 13. And F stays at 14, since going through H would cost 16. Check any of these by adding the edges along the final path. Keep your settled set, tentative distances, and tie policy all explicit, and it's mechanical.
Don't confuse the two sets. A tentative distance can keep improving. A settled one is final, and that's only guaranteed because weights aren't negative.
Return to our small graph, and change one number. Raise the cost of the link between B and C from 1 to 6. Everything else stays the same.
Run Dijkstra in your head. What are the three distances now? And which neighbor does A use to reach C?

Settle B at 2. Through B, C would now cost 8, which doesn't beat the direct 5. D becomes 6 through B. Then settle C at 5. Through C, D would cost 7, which doesn't beat 6. So the distances are 2, 5, and 6. A's first hop to B is B, to C is C itself, and to D is B. One number changed, and A's route to C changed completely. But before A could install this, the new cost had to reach it. Flooding carries the whole map to everyone. What if routers shared something much smaller instead?

Link state asks every router to store and process a map of the whole network. Could a router find good paths knowing almost nothing, just by asking its neighbors one simple question? How far are you from the destination?

That's distance-vector routing. No router keeps a map. Each one keeps a list of destinations and its best known distance to each, and it tells that list only to its direct neighbors. Then each router combines what its neighbors said with the cost of reaching them. It's like asking for directions. You can't see the route. But if your neighbor says they're 3 kilometers from the station, and they are 3 kilometers from you, then you know something about your own distance.

Compute one. A's link to B costs 3, and B says it's 3 away from Z. That's a total of 6. A's link to C costs 2, and C says 5. That's a total of 7. The minimum is 6, through B. So A's distance is 6, and its next hop is B. A doesn't know B's internal path to Z, and it doesn't need to. Now B advertises something new: its distance is 10. Through B would now cost 13. Through C still costs 7. So A switches to C, and its table changes with no map in sight.

The rule, called the Bellman-Ford update. x is me. y is the destination. v ranges over my neighbors. My distance to y is the minimum, over all neighbors v, of my link cost to v, plus v's advertised distance to y. And the neighbor that gives the minimum becomes my next hop. Two terms, and they come from different places. The first I can measure myself. The second I'm trusting my neighbor about.

How does a whole network find its answers? Knowledge spreads in rounds. Use our graph from before, and an idealized synchronous exercise: in each round, every router uses only the advertisements from the previous round. In round one, each router knows just itself and its direct neighbors. So A has B at 2, C at 5, and D at infinity.

Round two. A hears B's vector from round one. B says it's 1 from C, and 4 from D. So through B, C costs 2 plus 1, which is 3. And D costs 2 plus 4, which is 6. A's table now reflects paths of up to two edges.

Here's the subtle step. During round two, B also heard from C, and learned it can reach D for 1 plus 2, which is 3. In round three, B advertises that better number. A computes 2 plus 3, which is 5, through B. It has discovered the path A, B, C, D, without ever knowing that C was involved. The next round changes nothing, so it has converged, on the same answers Dijkstra gave.

Those neat rounds are a classroom picture. Real routers update whenever they like, with no global clock. A value from a neighbor could also be old, not a final truth. RIP and EIGRP are the named members of this family. RIP uses hop count as its metric. Don't assume EIGRP behaves identically, because its rules differ in detail.

Classify them. OSPF and IS-IS belong with link state. RIP and EIGRP belong with distance vector. RIP gives each link a hop cost of 1, so usable distances run from 1 to 15, and 16 means unreachable. Only RIP has that limit, as far as this lecture shows, so don't carry it over to EIGRP.

Compare what's being trusted. Link state trusts link facts, and computes its own paths. Distance vector trusts its neighbors' computed results. Both reach shortest paths with a shared metric. But they share different knowledge, and that decides how they behave when things break. The reusable distinction is simple: a map, versus neighbors' distances.

The lecture adds a broad comparison, and you should treat it as a family-level teaching picture, rather than a universal benchmark. Link state sends more messages, since facts flood everywhere, and each router runs its own computation. If one router computes something wrong, that error stays mostly local. Distance vector exchanges only with its neighbors. But a wrong number is passed along as if it were a fact, so one router's error can spread through everyone's tables. Real costs depend on graph size and on protocol details.
In a synchronous trace, here's where marks get lost. Every router computes from the previous round's advertisements. Mixing in values from the current round changes the answer.
You do one. Router x has two neighbors. Its link to P costs 4, and P advertises 7 to the destination. Its link to Q costs 9, and Q advertises 1.
Which neighbor wins? Then suppose P's link cost rises to 6. Does your answer change?

P gives 11, and Q gives 10, so Q wins, even though its link is the expensive one. Raise P's link to 6, and P only gets worse, at 13, so Q still wins. Notice that the router is relying on a number somebody else told it. It has no way to know how that number was produced, and no way to know whether the path behind it runs right back through itself. We'll come back to exactly that danger. First, there's one situation where neither of these approaches works at all.

Between organizations, neither method fits. Would your company publish its internal map to its competitors, as link state needs? Would it accept a single cost number from them, whose meaning it can't check? Networks run by different owners need something else.

Consider why each one breaks down. Link state floods topology, which reveals private structure, and it requires a common metric. Distance vector hides the structure, so it's on the right track. But one bare number has two problems. Different networks measure cost differently, so the numbers aren't comparable. And the number hides the route, so nobody can apply a preference such as, avoid that competitor.

The fix is to advertise the whole path. Instead of saying, I'm 3 away, a network says, I can reach it through networks 3, 2, 1. Each network that passes this along adds its own identifier at the front. This is path-vector routing, and it's the basis of BGP.

Benefit one is easy loop detection. Say AS 3 offers the path 3, 2, 1 back to AS 1. AS 1 looks through the list, sees itself, and rejects it. It doesn't need to count, or wait. The loop is visible right there in the data.

Benefit two is policy. Now that you can see the whole route, you can apply your own judgment. A network may prefer a longer path, for business reasons. It may avoid one that crosses a particular network. It may decide not to pass a route on to some neighbor. There's no shared definition of best anymore. That flexibility is the point. But it also means that loop-free does not imply everyone's choices fit together. We'll return to that.
Don't overclaim here. Rejecting paths that contain your own AS stops loops. It doesn't promise immediate convergence, and it doesn't rule out policy oscillation.
Test the rule. AS 4 receives the path 3, 2, 1. Next, AS 2 receives the path 3, 4, 2, 1. And then AS 5 is offered a path of length two and a path of length five.
Which paths get rejected as loops? And must AS 5 choose the shorter one?

AS 4 accepts: it isn't in the list. AS 2 rejects: its own number appears. And AS 5 may take either one. Its local policy can prefer the longer path. Path vector tells it what's possible, and it decides what's best. One routing idea remains in this lecture, and it asks a different question. Once a path is known, must every router really look up the address all over again?

Every router on a path repeats a longest prefix match, for the very same packet. And all traffic to one destination follows the shortest path, even when another route has spare capacity. Could we set up a path in advance, and just follow it?

That's what MPLS does. At the edge of the network, an ingress router classifies the packet, and pushes a short label in front of the IP header. Routers inside read only the label, and look it up in a small exact table. The label says which prepared path this packet is on. The last router pops the label, and ordinary IP takes over.

Labels only have local meaning. Label 17 reaches R2, whose table says: incoming 17, swap to 42, and send on this interface. Then R3 sees 42, and its table says to pop. Each router picks its own numbers, so the label changes at each hop while the path stays fixed. Does that remind you of something? The label behaves just like the yellow envelope. Only the IP header stays the same throughout.

Who installed those table entries? Signaling. Before any data flows, messages travel along the chosen path, setting up state at each router. The lecture names RSVP, and for MPLS traffic engineering, the specific extension is RSVP-TE. Because the path is explicit, an operator can steer some traffic away from the shortest route, onto spare capacity. That is traffic engineering.

See what that buys. With ordinary IP, two packets for the same destination take the same route from any given router, because they match the same prefix. With labels, an ingress router can place them on different prepared paths. The original motive for MPLS included faster lookup. Today, traffic engineering is the bigger reason.

Remember what a label path is, and what it is not. It's prepared forwarding state. It doesn't by itself reserve bandwidth, and it doesn't make delivery reliable. Something must still decide what state to install, and that's the control plane again.

Back to our laptop's packet. At every router on the way to the server, it now finds a table entry, built from a shared map, from neighbors' distances, or from paths. Where MPLS is in use, it may even carry a label for part of the way. The packet itself never knew any of this happened.
A label alone doesn't reserve anything. It's just how a router finds the next step. Reserving capacity takes signaling, and not every MPLS deployment uses it.
Change the question. R2's own table reuses label 17 for a totally different path, on another interface. And a packet with label 99 arrives at R2, where no entry exists.
Is reusing 17 a conflict? And can the router just fall back to searching the label space for the packet with 99?

Reuse isn't automatically a conflict, because labels are local, and each entry's scope is defined by its table. Different routers routinely reuse the same number. A label with no matching state has no installed instruction, so it has no valid forwarding action. State has to exist before it can be used. And that raises this chapter's biggest question. We've treated every table as correct and complete. What really happens in the seconds after a link fails?

A backhoe cuts a fiber between two routers. A moment before, every table was correct. A few seconds later, every table will be correct again. So what happens to our laptop's packets during those few seconds? The answer shows that correct before and correct after does not mean safe in between.

Picture our laptop's video call, running happily through R1 and R2. The packets keep coming every few milliseconds, whether the tables are ready or not. So a failure isn't an abstract event. It happens underneath traffic that's already moving.

First, what kinds of change are we talking about? Some are planned: maintenance that shuts down a link, or traffic engineering that changes a weight. Others aren't: a fiber cut, a power failure, or crashing software. Keep this separate from a different problem we'll reach later. A new route to the same location is a routing change. A host moving to a new location is mobility. Here, the destination stays put, and the network underneath it changes.

First, how does anyone even find out? Sometimes the hardware reports a dead link. Often routers exchange periodic hello messages, and declare a neighbor dead after a few are missed. That leaves a real tension. A short timer finds failures quickly, but it costs more traffic and processing, and it can raise false alarms, since a delayed hello looks exactly like a dead neighbor. A long timer is calm, and slow.

Detection is just the start, and it's local. Everybody else must then be told. Routing convergence is the whole transition, and it has four stages. Detect the change. Spread the news. Compute new routes. Install them in forwarding tables. If those take 30, 10, 5, and 15 milliseconds in sequence, the total is 60 milliseconds. Real stages can overlap, and each router's clock runs differently. But name the stages, before you blame the algorithm.

Watch the packets. A forwards traffic for D to B, and B forwards to D. The link from B to D fails. B knows, but A hasn't heard. A keeps sending to B, on its old and perfectly reasonable route. B has nothing usable, and those packets vanish. That's a forwarding blackhole. Note that A has not computed anything wrong. It's just working from old information.

B computes a new route for D. It goes back through A, then C, then D. And B installs that first, while A still points to B. So look at what happens now. A sends the packet to B. B sends it back to A. They bounce it between them. The old configuration had no loop. The new configuration has no loop. The mix of the two does. This is a transient forwarding loop. It isn't specific to any one protocol, and it can happen with link state, whenever routers install their changes at different times.

What does IP's TTL do here? It eventually kills the looping packet, but it doesn't save it, and until then, the loop eats up link capacity. Other packets may arrive out of order when old and new paths have different delays. So an application can suffer, even if a perfectly good alternate path exists the whole time.

To improve convergence, work stage by stage. Detect faster. Send control messages promptly. Compute incrementally. Install changes efficiently. And keep the principle in mind: a faster processor cannot make up for waiting minutes to declare a neighbor dead. Find the slowest stage first.
A tempting thought: both the old tables and the new tables are correct, so no harm done. But correct before and after protects nobody in between. Packets can vanish or loop during the transition.
Change the install order. Same failure, same routers, but this time A installs its new route first, and goes through C directly. Then B installs its route, by way of A.
