With that order, is there a loop? Is there still a blackhole, at any moment?

No loop forms, because A no longer sends to B. Traffic from A goes straight to C and D. Packets that reach B in the gap before it installs can still be lost, so B's own blackhole lasts until it updates. Ordering changes which disruption you get. These problems come from timing, and they pass quickly. But one protocol family can make things far worse: nobody gets told the truth for a very long time.

Distance vector routers believe the numbers their neighbors tell them. When a link gets cheaper, that's wonderful. When a link fails, it's a disaster, and the reason is not obvious. Why should good news travel fast, while bad news crawls?

Start with good news. A link cost drops. The router attached to it sees a better distance, tells its neighbor, who sees a better distance too, and tells the next. The improvement spreads in a couple of exchanges, and everyone stops. A real, better path exists, so every update is true.

The bad news, on this tiny chain. Y reaches X directly, at distance 1. Z reaches X through Y, at distance 2. And there is no other route to X in this network at all. Now cut the link between X and Y. X is gone. Y knows immediately. What should it do? It looks at what its neighbors have advertised, and it sees Z saying, I can reach X at distance 2.

The trap. Y has no way of knowing that Z's path runs through Y itself. A bare number hides that. So Y believes it. Z's 2 plus a link of 1 makes 3, and Y now routes to X through Z. Y tells Z the news: I'm at 3. Z depends on Y, so Z updates: 3 plus 1 is 4. Z tells Y. Y updates: 5. Then Z: 6.

Stop and see what those numbers mean. There is no path to X at all. Yet each router is confident. They point at each other, and their traffic bounces between them, while the numbers creep up, until they reach whatever the protocol treats as infinity. No new links appeared. The routers are slowly unlearning something false. This is called count to infinity. It's information feedback, not any physical growth in the network. And a cost increase can trigger the same counting, even if a real but expensive alternate exists. They just count up until the alternate wins.

One crude fix is to make infinity small. RIP treats 16 as unreachable, leaving 1 through 15 as usable metrics. Now the counting stops at 16, soon rather than never. But any network wider than 15 hops can't be represented. And the underlying problem has not gone anywhere. We only bounded it.

A better fix targets the actual lie. Go back to before the failure. Z's route to X goes through Y. So why would Z ever tell Y that it has a route to X? That information is useless to Y, and we've just seen that it's dangerous. Poison reverse says: if you route through a neighbor, tell that neighbor your distance is infinity. Z keeps its true route, and tells Y infinity. It can still tell its other neighbors the truth. So the advertisement is specific to each neighbor. It is not a command to delete anything.

Replay the failure. X and Y lose their link. Y checks its neighbors. Z says infinity. So Y knows it has nowhere to go, and it tells Z so. Z's only route was through Y, so Z drops to infinity as well. Done, in one quick exchange, with no counting.

See the counting itself with the slide's real numbers, on a slightly bigger network. X to Y costs 4, Y to Z costs 1, and X to Z costs 50. Y reaches X directly at 4, and Z goes through Y, at 5. Now suppose X to Y gets better, dropping to 1. Y's distance falls to 1, and it tells Z. Z computes 2. Z tells Y, and Y stays at 1. Done, in two exchanges.

Make it worse, raising X to Y from 4 to 60. Y compares a direct cost of 60 with Z's old claim of 5, through a link of 1, for a total of 6. It picks 6, through Z, not knowing that Z's 5 ran through Y. Z hears 6, and computes 7. Y hears 7, and computes 8.

They climb 2 at a time, while packets for X bounce between them. It only ends when going through Y costs more than Z's real direct link of 50. Then Z settles at 50, and Y at 51. That took more than twenty exchanges, for one changed number. Without the 50 link, it would never stop on its own.
Making infinity small feels like a fix. It isn't. It only bounds the counting, and it limits how wide the network can be. The underlying dependency is still there.
Is the problem solved? Add a third router to the loop. Now Y, Z, and W form a triangle, and they all reach X through Y. Z and W are each other's neighbors.
Z poisons its route toward Y. But what does Z tell W? Could W now give Y bad advice?

Z tells W the truth: distance 2. It doesn't route through W, so it has no reason to poison. W then thinks it has a path to X through Z, and it can tell Y. So a loop of three can still count up. Poison reverse handles the simple two-node case, not every cycle. What's the real issue? The number hides the path. So what if routers just sent the path? That's the fix BGP uses, and we'll see that even this doesn't make the trouble go away.

Path vector carries the whole path, so a router can spot a loop at once, and count to infinity disappears. Does that mean convergence is solved? There are two remaining problems. It can be slow in a new way. And even worse, with some policies, it may never settle at all.

First, how do BGP neighbors notice that one of them has died? BGP runs over a TCP connection, and TCP alone won't tell you that an idle peer has vanished. So neighbors send keepalive messages. In the slide's example, a keepalive goes every 60 seconds, and the hold timer is 180 seconds. If nothing arrives for that long, the session is declared dead. Every route learned over it is then invalid. So just detecting one failure may take three minutes.

Suppose destination 0 disappears entirely. Follow AS 2 as the news spreads. It's been using the direct path, 2, 0. That gets withdrawn. But it remembers an alternative through AS 1: 2, 1, 0. It looks fine, it's loop-free, and it's false, since AS 1 simply hasn't heard yet. Then that's withdrawn too. So it tries 2, 3, 0, which is also stale. Next 2, 1, 3, 0, longer still. Only after all of those does it finally have no route. This is path exploration. Each candidate seems reasonable locally, and each fails in turn. Every step also causes more update messages.

Why doesn't that settle faster? Each router must first hear about the failure of what it's using, then choose its next best candidate, and advertise that. Those messages are limited by timers, so that routers aren't flooded with updates. So each wrong candidate can take a while to be discovered. Also, not every BGP change is a hardware failure. Import and export policy changes, resets of sessions, and persistent instability all make routes change too.

The deeper problem. Each network ranks paths by its own policy. Do those independent choices always fit together? To study this, there's a clean model called the stable paths problem. Each node has a ranked list of permitted paths to destination 0. A path is available only if the next hop is actually using exactly the rest of that path. A stable assignment gives every node its best available path, all at the same time.

Solve the instructor's instance. Node 3 has only one permitted path, 30, so it uses it. Node 1 prefers 130, and since 3 uses 30, that's available, so node 1 uses 130. Node 2 prefers 210, which requires node 1 to use 10. But node 1 uses 130, so that's unavailable, and node 2 falls back to 20.

Node 4 prefers 420, and node 2 does use 20, so 420 works. Node 5 allows only 5210. That needs node 2 on 210, which it isn't. So node 5 has no path, even though it's physically connected to node 2. The slide asks two questions. Will node 1 use a direct path? False. Does node 5 have a path? False.

That instance has exactly one solution. Others don't. Take two nodes, each preferring to reach the destination through the other. Node 1 likes 120 best, and node 2 likes 210 best. There are two stable outcomes. Node 1 goes through node 2, while 2 goes direct. Or the reverse. Which one you get depends on who speaks first. Same policies, same links, different result.

Three nodes in a ring. Each prefers the path through its clockwise neighbor, and each will otherwise go direct. Try to settle them. If node 1 goes direct, node 2 can use its favorite, through node 1, and so node 2 is not direct. Then node 3 can't use 320, and goes direct. But then node 1 can use 130, its favorite, and is no longer direct. That undoes node 2's choice. And round it goes. An exhaustive check of every assignment finds no stable solution at all. No link failed. Policies alone keep routes changing, forever. That's policy oscillation.

For our laptop, all of this shows up as a stall or a gap. Its video freezes for a moment, and then recovers. The laptop did nothing wrong, and neither did its server. The network was changing its mind, or couldn't settle it.
The trap with path exploration. A path with no AS loop can still be stale. No loop is a much weaker claim than, this path is still available now.
Change one line of policy. Node 3 decides it will no longer prefer the path through node 2. It now ranks going direct first, with 320 second.
Does that single change produce a stable solution? Work it out starting from node 3.

Yes. Node 3 uses 30, and never moves. So node 1's favorite, 130, is always available, and node 1 uses it. Node 2 then can't use 210, and so it goes direct, on 20. Everyone's happy, and nothing changes. One local preference broke the cycle. So the trouble isn't BGP's messages, it's the combination of rankings. Then what real-world force keeps the Internet's policies from forming these cycles? The answer is money. Let us see how BGP really works, and how business relationships shape it.

Our laptop's packet to the web server has so far crossed two friendly routers. On the real Internet, it would cross networks owned by companies that compete with each other, each one keeping its internal design private, and each one with its own idea of what a good route means. How can those rivals still cooperate well enough to deliver a packet? There's exactly one protocol doing this job across the whole planet, and we need to see what it actually says.

Our laptop's server sits in a different network from the laptop, run by a different company. Everything we've built so far works inside one organization. So who tells R2's network that the server's prefix even exists, and why would they agree to carry it?

A little context. The Internet's interdomain routing protocol is BGP, and it's been in use, in revised versions, since the early days of the commercial Internet. It's a path-vector protocol, the very idea from chapter 6. Now we can fill in how it really works.

The unit of cooperation is the autonomous system, or AS. That's a set of networks under one routing administration, identified by a number. A university, an Internet provider, or a content company can each be an AS. Inside, it may run many routers, using OSPF or IS-IS, and that's nobody else's business. From the outside, we draw it as a single cloud. This is an abstraction with a price, which we'll get to in a moment.

BGP, the Border Gateway Protocol, is what those clouds speak to each other. Two routers open a TCP connection on port 179, called a session. First they exchange all their active routes. After that they send only changes: announcements of new routes, and withdrawals of old ones. That makes it an incremental protocol. It's also prefix based, so what it advertises is reachability to a block of addresses, like 203.0.113.0/24, not to individual machines.

What exactly is a BGP route? It's a prefix, plus attributes. Two matter most right now. AS PATH is the list of autonomous systems the route has passed through. NEXT HOP says which IP address to send toward. Watch how the path grows. AS 300 owns the prefix, and it tells AS 200 the path is just 300. AS 200 adds itself, and tells AS 100 that the path is 200, 300.

Inside that list is our loop check from before. A receiving AS looks for its own number, and if it's there, the route is rejected. That handles one kind of consistency. We've already seen that it doesn't prevent path exploration or policy oscillation.

The price of the abstraction. Is a shorter AS path a shorter route? Not necessarily. Here are two options. One crosses 2 ASes, but each contains a long chain of routers. The other crosses 3 ASes, each with only one or two routers. Measured in router hops, the 3 AS path is the shorter of the two. And it says nothing at all about delay. AS path length counts organizations, not distance.
Don't read too much into AS path length. It counts networks, not routers. It says nothing about latency or capacity, and prepending can make it artificial.
You try. AS 200 gets an offer of 300, 500. It passes that along to AS 100, and AS 500 is also a neighbor of AS 100. Suppose AS 100 then re-advertises its path to AS 500.
What is the path list when it reaches AS 500? And what will AS 500 do with it?

AS 500 receives 100, 200, 300, 500. It sees its own number at the end, and it rejects the route. Notice one thing we still haven't said: when AS 100 has several acceptable routes, how does it pick? And who decides which neighbors hear about the choice? That isn't physics, and it isn't shortest paths. It's policy.

A neighbor hands you a route. Do you have to believe it? Do you have to use it? If you use it, must you tell everyone else? With BGP, the answer to all three questions is no. Those are three separate decisions, and getting them apart is the key to the whole protocol.

The pipeline in every BGP router. Routes arrive from neighbors. Import policy filters them, and may change their attributes. Best-route selection picks one route per prefix for use. That route goes into forwarding. Then export policy decides, separately for each neighbor, what to advertise. Because the stages are separate, a route rejected at import never becomes a candidate. A route suppressed at export can still be the one you use yourself.

Import first. Why would you ever reject a route? Say your customer owns one prefix, and suddenly announces a route to a big video site. That's either a configuration mistake, or an attack. Believing it would pull the world's traffic into your customer's network. So on a session to a customer, a network commonly accepts only the prefixes that customer actually holds. An advertisement is data to evaluate, not an order.

Import can also attach a value called local preference. It's a number used only inside your own AS, and higher is better. It's checked before anything else, so it directly states your own ranking. For example, you might set 100 on routes from a customer, and 90 on routes from a peer, because customers pay you, and carrying traffic to them earns money. Compare. A customer route with local preference 100 and an AS path of 4, against a peer route with local preference 90 and an AS path of 2. The customer route wins. Length is never even looked at.

The other end of the pipeline. Export policy decides what each neighbor gets to hear. Why not tell everyone everything? Because telling a neighbor about a route is an offer: send your traffic through me, and I'll carry it. Advertising a route is promising to do work. So a network can use a route itself, while deliberately keeping it from a neighbor. Using a route and offering transit are different acts.

Export can also change how a route looks. Suppose you have two links to the Internet, and want incoming traffic on just one of them. You can't control anybody else's decision. But you can make one option look worse. AS path prepending repeats your own number. Instead of announcing 300, you announce 300, 300, 300 over the backup link. Remote networks comparing path lengths will tend to choose the other link. Tend to, because prepending can't force anything. A remote network's local preference is checked first, and it could still ignore you.

Keep these two tools straight. Local preference ranks routes within your own AS, and it controls your outgoing traffic. Prepending changes what others see, so it only influences your incoming traffic. One is a decision. The other is a suggestion.

Where do all these policies live? Administrators write them, per neighbor, in router configuration. That's a lot of manual work, spread over many routers and many people, and mistakes do happen. A configuration error can be visible across the entire Internet.
A common mistake is to weigh these numbers against each other. There's no trade between preference and path length. Preference is compared first, and length matters only if preference ties.

A situation. Network A prepends heavily on its link to provider P, hoping traffic will arrive by way of provider Q instead. But a far-off network, Z, assigns a high local preference to routes learned through P.
Which way does Z's traffic arrive at A? And did the prepending do anything at all?

It arrives through P, the path A was trying to discourage, because Z compares local preference first, and never reaches the length comparison. Prepending may still influence others who have tied preferences. So that's the outside view of an AS. But an AS isn't really one node. It's a set of routers with their own geography. How do they agree on what to do?

We've been drawing each AS as a dot. But a large provider has hundreds of routers across a continent, and it may hear about the same destination at several different border routers. How do all its internal routers learn about that, and how does each one pick an exit?

A BGP session between different ASes is called eBGP, for external. A session between routers within the same AS is iBGP, for internal. Here's the flow. Border router R1 learns a route over eBGP. It passes this along to R2 and R3 over iBGP. Now all of them know the route. Note that internal routers don't add their AS number again as the update moves around inside.

And iBGP does not replace the internal routing protocol. It says that a destination is reachable through a certain exit. But it doesn't say how to get across your own network to that exit. That's still the job of OSPF or IS-IS. BGP and the IGP solve two halves of one problem.

How those halves are joined. BGP says: 203.0.113.0/24 has next hop 192.0.2.9. But that router may be several hops away. So the router looks up 192.0.2.9 in its internal routes, and finds it goes through neighbor 198.51.100.2 on port 3. It combines the two, and installs: 203.0.113.0/24 goes through 198.51.100.2 on port 3. A BGP next hop isn't necessarily a directly connected neighbor. It has to be resolved first.

Now the decision process can be stated in full, in the lecture's simplified order. Highest local preference. Then shortest AS path. Then lowest internal cost to the exit. Then a tie break. Compare in order, and stop as soon as one route remains. These are not added into a score. There's no formula that combines them.

Try three routes for one prefix. A has local preference 140, length 4, and exit cost 50. B has 100, length 2, and cost 5. C has 100, length 2, and cost 1. With all three available, A wins immediately on preference, despite being the worst by every other number. Withdraw A. B and C tie on preference, and tie on length, so internal cost decides: C wins. Now shorten B's path to length 1. B beats C at step two, and its higher exit cost never gets compared.

That third step has a nickname: hot-potato routing. When outside attributes tie, hand the traffic off at the nearest exit, and spend as little of your own network as possible. Picture a network with exits on the west and east coasts. A router with internal costs 4 and 9 picks west. A router on the other side, with costs 12 and 3, picks east. Each one minimizes its own carrying cost. And so the return path, chosen by a different network with its own hot potatoes, may take a different route. Internet paths are often asymmetric for just this reason.

Does every router need all those routes? No. A customer with a single provider has only one way out. It can use a default route: a slash 0, matching everything, pointing at the provider. Any longer prefix beats it. So a stub network, or an internal router at the edge, can hold a very small table. Full tables belong where real choices exist, not everywhere.
The classic confusion. A BGP next hop isn't necessarily the neighbor you hand the frame to. It can be several routers away, so it has to be resolved through internal routing.
Change the costs. Internal maintenance raises router R's cost to the west exit from 4 to 11. Its east cost stays at 9. Nothing outside the AS has changed.
Does R's exit change? And does some neighbor network now see traffic it wasn't seeing before?

Yes. R now prefers east, at 9. Its traffic moves to a different exit, and possibly to a different neighbor network. An internal change shifted traffic outside the AS. That's the coupling between BGP and the internal protocol. We've now covered how the decision works. But why do networks set these preferences in the first place? Because each link between two networks has a contract, and someone pays.

Networks are businesses. Carrying traffic costs money, and some of it pays and some doesn't. If you ran a network, whose traffic would you carry for free? Whose routes would you repeat? Those two business questions end up explaining most of Internet routing.

There are two main relationships. In a customer-provider link, the customer pays the provider for connectivity to the rest of the Internet. We draw the arrow pointing from customer up to provider. In peering, two networks exchange traffic, typically without payment, but only for themselves and their customers. A peer isn't offering you transit to the world. It's only offering you what's below it.

From these contracts comes one question that decides every export. Would this make me carry traffic between two networks, when neither is my customer? If a route came from a customer, or it's my own, then I tell everyone, because traffic toward it earns me money. If it came from a peer or a provider, I tell only my customers. Telling a provider about my peer's route would invite my provider to send traffic through me, to my peer, for free, while I pay for it. So read the table. Own and customer routes go everywhere. Peer and provider routes go only to customers.

Those contracts stack up into a structure. At the top are Tier 1 providers, with no upstream provider at all, connected to each other as peers. Below them are other providers, which sell transit to customers, but must buy it from someone. At the bottom are stub ASes, which provide no transit, and those are the vast majority. And this graph has a key property. It's directed and acyclic. If u is a customer of v, and v is a customer of w, then w isn't a customer of u. Remember that when we come to stability.

Those exports have a visible consequence in the data path. A permitted path climbs up through customer to provider links, crosses at most one peer link, and then descends through provider to customer links. It's up, peer, down. It's called valley free. Going down and then back up would be a valley: some customer would be carrying traffic between its two providers, paying both for the privilege. Nobody signs up for that.

Classify the instructor's paths, reading in the direction data travels. 1, 2, d: down, down. Valid. 7, d: up. Valid. 5, 8, d: 8 is 5's customer, so that's down, then up. A valley. Invalid, since 8 would carry traffic between its providers. 6, 4, 3, d: up, peer, down. Valid. 8, 5, d: up, peer. Valid. 6, 5, d: peer, peer. Invalid, because a path can have only one peer crossing. And 1, 4, 3, d: down, peer, down. Invalid, because the peer crossing comes after descending.

Look at two of those again. 5, 8, d is invalid. And 8, 5, d is valid. They use nearly the same networks, in a different direction. So direction matters, and the set of nodes alone tells you nothing. Build the relationship sequence, and read it, rather than memorizing node numbers.

The payoff, connecting to the oscillating ring from last chapter. Gao and Rexford showed that three commercial habits are enough for stability, under their model. One: the customer-provider hierarchy has no cycles, so nobody is their own provider's provider. Two: prefer customer routes over peer and provider routes. Three: follow the export rule we just saw. Why does the bad gadget disappear?

Its cycle needs each network to prefer a route through its neighbor, around a ring. Under these rules, that ring of preferences can't form. Those are sufficient conditions in the model. They aren't a claim that every BGP deployment follows them, or that every stable network must. Still, it's striking. No one coordinates globally. Each business pursues its own interest, and the system tends to settle.

Look at the whole path of our laptop's packet. It climbs from the laptop's provider, perhaps crosses one peer link, and descends to the server's provider. Contracts set that shape. The shortest path on a map had very little to do with it.
A short path in the drawing isn't necessarily a usable one. If export policy never advertised it, no traffic will follow it, however connected it looks.
A business decision. AS A has a peer P, a provider U, and a customer C. It learns a route from P. And it learns another route from its customer C.
Who hears about P's route from A? Who hears about C's route?

P's route goes only to customer C. Telling U would have A carrying traffic between its provider and its peer. C's route goes to everyone: U, P, and C itself has it already. That's exactly the reachability A is being paid to spread. So far, every packet has had one destination. But what if one address should mean several servers? Or what if a thousand receivers all want the same stream? Our next chapter changes who a destination is.

Our laptop has been talking to one server. But a popular service runs in many locations. DNS could return different addresses, but what happens if one of those servers fails? The laptop's cache keeps handing out the dead address until the TTL runs out. Could one single address lead to several servers, so a failure needs no new DNS answer at all?

So far, our laptop has sent to exactly one server. But when it looks up a popular name, which of a thousand servers should answer? And when it joins a live stream, what if a million other laptops want the same bits? The destination is about to stop meaning one machine.

See the limit first. A DNS answer may hold several A records, for load balancing and failover, each one valid for 300 seconds. If a server fails, clients can hold on to its address for that long. A very low TTL puts extra load on DNS, and browsers may cache addresses regardless. And what if the DNS server itself is the thing that fails? We can't use DNS to fail over DNS.

It can, and it takes no new protocol. Give two server instances the same address, 10.0.0.1, and let both locations announce it into routing. Routers simply see two routes to one destination. Router 1's table lists 10.0.0.1 through router 2 at distance 1, and through router 3 at distance 2. It chooses the closer one, just as it would for any route. That's IP anycast. One destination, delivered to one selected instance.

Instance A fails, and its route is withdrawn. The client does nothing. It keeps sending to the same address. Router 1 falls back to the remaining route, and packets now reach instance B. There's no new DNS answer, and no client change. But failover isn't instant. It still waits for health detection, and routing convergence. And ordinary routing knows nothing about server load, or whether the program behind a live route is actually healthy.

Here's the rule. Anycast means one of many, and routing picks which one. DNS still says just one thing, www.server.com is 10.0.0.1, and that answer stays true. Be aware that the slide's slash 32 is an internal toy example. Whether the wider Internet accepts a prefix that specific depends on routing policy.
The slide's warning is easy to overread. Anycast isn't banned for TCP. The real issue is that a flow might shift to an instance without its connection state.
Use anycast for something long-lived. A client has an open TCP connection to instance A. Routes shift, though nothing failed, and the next packet is delivered to instance B.
What does instance B do with that packet, and why?

B has never heard of this connection. It has no state for it, so the connection can break. That's the real meaning of the slide's warning. The problem is lost connection state, and anycast isn't flatly incompatible with TCP. Stable routing and careful service design make it workable. In fact, the DNS root servers we met earlier are deployed this way: 13 identities, with many anycast instances. Anycast picked one receiver out of many. Next, what if we want all of them?

A source wants to send one 10 megabit per second stream to three receivers. All three sit behind the same first link. Must that link really carry three identical copies? And how would the network even know who wants the stream?

The simple answer is iterated unicast. Just send a separate copy to each receiver. It needs no network support at all. But on the shared link, that's 3 times 10, or 30 megabits per second, all carrying the same bits.
Scale it up. A one megabyte file sent separately to 100 receivers makes the sender transmit 100 megabytes. If every copy crosses the same upstream link, that link carries all 100.

IP multicast does better. The source sends one copy, addressed to a group, and routers replicate it only where paths diverge. The shared link carries just 10 megabits per second. The saving is on the shared edges. There's still forwarding work at each branch. And notice the difference from anycast. Anycast reaches one of many. Multicast reaches all who are interested.

What goes in the packet? The sender keeps its ordinary source address. The destination is a group address, drawn from 224.0.0.0/4. That address names no single machine, only an audience. A sender doesn't have to be a member. And the group's membership can change at any time.

A concrete example. A sender at 192.0.2.10 sends to group 239.1.1.1, and two receivers join that group. The packet's source stays 192.0.2.10, and its destination is 239.1.1.1. The source never becomes the group address.

What if routers don't support multicast? Overlay multicast builds the distribution tree among the end hosts themselves, using ordinary unicast. Each host receives the stream, and forwards it to a few others. It needs no router support. But overlay paths can cross the same physical link repeatedly, and forwarding uses up the hosts' upload capacity.
Picture it as a tree of hosts. The source sends to two peers, and each of them sends to two more. Seven recipients fit in three levels, and no router needs to know anything about the group.

Who's interested? IGMP handles this on the local network, between hosts and their directly attached router. The router sends a query: any members out there? Hosts reply with reports. Here's a clever trick. H1 and H2 both want group G. Each picks a random delay, say 2 seconds and 6 seconds. H1's timer fires first, and it sends its report to the group itself. H2 hears the report, and cancels its own. Why? Because the router only needs to know that someone on this LAN wants G, not who, or how many. In version 1 there's no leave message. Membership simply expires when reports stop.

The slides speak loosely here, so let's be exact. In version 1, queries go to the all-hosts group, and a report goes to the group being reported. That's how H2 hears H1's report. Both are limited to the local network with a TTL of 1.

Version 2 adds an explicit leave. When a host leaves, can the router stop forwarding at once? No. Another host on the LAN may still want the group. So the router sends a group-specific query to check. If H2 still cares, its report keeps the branch alive. Version 2 also adds querier election. Version 3 adds source filtering, so a host can say: I want group G, but only from source S.

A timer detail, with a clarification. The slide computes a timeout as 2 times the sum of 125 and 10, which gives 270 seconds. The standard's default formula, in RFC 2236, is 2 times 125, plus 10, which gives 260 seconds. If a question supplies the slide's formula, use it, and say so. Just don't quietly swap one for the other.

Finally, what about the switch? An ordinary switch floods multicast out every port. IGMP snooping lets it listen in on these membership messages, and deliver only to ports with interested hosts. So keep the scope clear. IGMP is about one local network. It doesn't build the tree between routers.

Say only one port has a receiver for a group. A snooping switch sends that group's traffic toward that port, and toward its router ports, rather than every access port. This is separate from unicast MAC learning, because it comes from reading membership messages.
Keep the scope straight. IGMP tells the last router which groups are wanted on its LAN. It doesn't compute the tree between routers. That's a multicast routing protocol's job.
Change the numbers. A 5 megabit stream, three receivers behind one shared link, with report delays of 2, 5, and 8 seconds.
What's the load on the shared link, with unicast versus multicast? And how many reports does the router actually hear?

Unicast loads the link with 15 megabits per second. Multicast with 5. And the router hears only one report, at 2 seconds, because the others suppress theirs. So local interest is known. But how does the data cross many routers, to reach all those interested networks? We need a tree. And it turns out the word tree can mean several different things.

To deliver to many networks, routers need a tree. But we've already met one tree in spanning tree, and another in Dijkstra's. Are they the same? What does best even mean for a tree? And should every sender get its own tree, or should they all share one?

First, a split. A source-based tree is rooted at one sender, so state is kept per source and group, written S comma G. A shared tree is used by all senders in the group, written star comma G. A shared tree needs less state. Source trees can give shorter paths. So we're trading memory against path quality.

Next, objectives. A minimum spanning tree connects all nodes with the smallest total edge cost. There are two classic ways to find one. Prim's algorithm grows one tree outward, always adding the cheapest edge that crosses from the tree to a node outside. Kruskal's algorithm sorts all edges, and adds each one unless it would create a cycle. Try this triangle: A to B is 1, B to C is 1, and A to C is 1 point 5. Both algorithms choose A B and B C, for a total of 2.

Ask a different question. What's the shortest way from A to C? It's the direct edge, at 1 point 5, which isn't even in that tree. Dijkstra's tree from A would use it. So three things share the word tree. STP makes layer 2 forwarding loop-free. An MST minimizes total edge cost. A shortest path tree minimizes distance from one source. Same word, different objectives.

One more design: core-based trees. Pick one router as the meeting point, called the core. Each receiver's router sends a join toward the core, and that request stops as soon as it hits a router already on the tree. Traffic then flows along those branches. It's simple and uses little state. But the core could become a hot spot, and paths may take a detour through it.
The sharing. Receiver routers A and B both join toward the core, and their paths merge at M. So the branch from the core to M carries one copy, and M replicates it toward the two receivers.
These algorithms look alike, and they aren't. Dijkstra accumulates distance from a source. Prim just picks the cheapest edge reaching the growing tree. The resulting trees can differ.
Change one cost. Make the direct A to C edge cost 0 point 5.
What's the minimum spanning tree now, and its total cost? And what's the shortest path tree from A?

The MST takes A C at 0 point 5, plus one of the edges of cost 1, for a total of 1 point 5. There's a tie, so either A B or B C works. From A, the shortest path tree uses A C and A B. So this time the two objectives can coincide, on one of the valid MSTs. They just don't have to. Real multicast protocols don't compute a global MST. They use something cheaper, already sitting in every router: the unicast routing table.

A router receives a multicast packet. If it floods the packet out every port, loops and duplicates will multiply, and we saw how badly that ends on Ethernet. How can a router decide whether to accept a packet, without any tree having been computed?

An elegant trick. Look at where the packet came from, and ask: if I were sending a packet back to this source, which port would I use? If the packet arrived on that port, it probably came along the shortest path. Accept it, and forward it out the other ports. If it arrived anywhere else, it's a duplicate that wandered around another branch. Drop it. That's reverse path forwarding. Say router X reaches source S through port 1. A packet from S arriving on port 1 passes. A copy arriving on port 3 fails.

RPF alone still sends data everywhere, as a broadcast with no duplicates. Let's narrow it. Truncated reverse path broadcasting skips a leaf LAN when IGMP says no members exist there. That removes only the last hop. Reverse path multicasting goes further. If a router has no local members, and none of its downstream routers want the data, it sends a prune upstream. Prunes propagate, so entire uninterested subtrees drop out.

PIM, protocol independent multicast, is the standard router protocol. It's called independent because it reuses whatever unicast routing is available. PIM dense mode is the approach we've just seen. Flood, then prune. Everything is forwarded unless a branch opts out. That's sensible if most networks want the data, but wasteful if very few do. Prunes also expire, so the flooding comes back periodically.

When receivers are rare, we flip the default. In PIM sparse mode, nothing flows until someone asks. Everyone agrees on a meeting point for the group, called the rendezvous point, or RP. A receiver's designated router sends a star comma G join toward the RP, creating a shared tree. Data then flows only along the branches that joined. The slide's phrase, CBT, source based, is shorthand. What actually happens is that sparse mode starts with this shared tree.

A source appears. Its designated router doesn't know the receivers. It only knows the RP. So it wraps the first data packets in a PIM Register message, and unicasts those to the RP. That's encapsulation again. The RP unwraps them, and sends them down the shared tree. Then the RP can set up native forwarding from the source, so that encapsulation is no longer needed.

Why wrap it at all? The source's router knows only the RP, and the RP hasn't built a path back yet. So Register is a bootstrap. The RP can unwrap each packet and send it down the shared tree, while native forwarding toward the source is being set up. A Register is not a join, and it's not a host's IGMP report.

But there's a problem: the RP might be far out of the way. Say source to RP costs 8, RP to receiver costs 7, and the direct path costs only 4. The receiver's router can now join toward the source, using S comma G. Once data arrives on the new path, it prunes this source from the RP branch. The cost drops from 15 to 4, a saving of 11. The group address stays the same. This is called SPT switchover. Start with a shared tree for easy discovery, then optimize.

There are two axes. Dense mode says: forward by default, and prune. Sparse mode says: send nothing until joined. And on any tree, RPF checks the upstream direction, while pruning trims the downstream outputs. IGMP tells the last router who is interested, and PIM connects the routers.

Set the two modes side by side. Dense mode starts broad, and shrinks. It needs no meeting point, but it pays with periodic flooding, and state in routers that have no interest. Sparse mode starts empty, and grows. It needs an RP, and it starts with possible detours, but quiet parts of the network never hear about the group at all. IP multicast is still best effort throughout, and neither mode makes it reliable.

For our laptop, joining a stream is simple. It sends one IGMP report to its local router. Everything else, the joins, the RP, the tree, happens in routers it never hears about. And if it stops listening, those branches get pruned away.
A group address has no location to route toward. The reverse path check asks about the source, or the tree's root: would I reach it through the port this packet came in on?
Change the geography. Suppose the RP sits right next to the path. Source to RP costs 2, RP to receiver costs 3, and the direct path costs 5.
What does a switchover save now? And is the RP then a hot spot, or a bargain?

Nothing at all. 2 plus 3 equals the direct 5. Switching would add state, for no shorter path. So the shared tree is not inherently bad. The cost of the detour depends on where the RP sits. That finishes our wired story. Packets have reached one host, one of many, and all who asked. But now the laptop unplugs from its wire, and all those assumptions about who can hear whom begin to fall apart.

Our laptop leaves the wire. Everything above the link layer still works, in principle. Yet on radio, a frame that was perfect at the sender may be garbage at the receiver, and the sender may have no idea. What actually changes when the wire goes away?

First, separate two ideas people often mix up. Wireless is about the medium: communicating over a radio link. Mobility is about changing your point of attachment. A fixed sensor is wireless, without being mobile. A laptop moved between wired subnets is mobile, without being wireless. This chapter is about the radio problem. The next is about movement.

Networks also differ in structure. In infrastructure mode, hosts talk through a base station, such as a Wi-Fi access point or a cell tower, that connects into the wired network. In ad hoc mode, there's no base station, and the nodes organize themselves. And either kind can be single hop or multiple hops, as in a mesh network, where traffic is relayed through other wireless nodes. Two independent questions: is there infrastructure, and how many wireless hops?

The slides chart radio technologies by rate and range, from Bluetooth at a couple of megabits per second, up through Wi-Fi and cellular generations. Those numbers belong to that era, and aren't promises about today's products. What lasts is the pattern. Higher rates tend to mean shorter range, and every link faces the same questions about frequency, coverage, and sharing.

The channel. Three separate things degrade a radio signal. Path loss: the signal weakens with distance, and when passing through obstacles. Interference: other transmitters and devices add competing energy, since many of them share frequencies like 2 point 4 gigahertz. And multipath: the signal bounces off walls and the ground, so delayed copies arrive at different times, and overlap with each other. An application may see the same symptom from all three, a lost packet, but they aren't the same mechanism.

To measure signal quality, we compare signal power to noise power. That's the signal to noise ratio, in decibels: 10 times log base 10 of signal over noise. A power ratio of 100 is 20 decibels. Higher SNR means fewer errors. The result is called bit error rate, or BER: the fraction of bits received wrong. These curves show the tradeoff. At the same SNR, a low-rate, robust scheme gives very few errors, while a high-rate scheme fails.

A radio link can't just pick one rate and stick to it. As a host moves away, SNR falls, and errors climb. Rate adaptation lowers the physical rate, moving to a more robust scheme. Raw rate is not goodput. Repeated failures at a high rate can deliver less than steady success at a low rate. And why not just raise the power? That burns energy, and it interferes with everybody else.
The rule is, the link's capacity isn't a fixed number. It depends on distance, surroundings, and everyone else who's transmitting at this moment.
Turning up the power seems like an easy fix for a weak signal. But it drains the battery, and it raises interference for everyone nearby.
Try the arithmetic. A receiver's signal is 1,000 times stronger than the noise. Then the laptop walks behind a wall, and the ratio drops to 10.
What are those two values, in decibels? And what should the sender do after the drop?

1,000 is 30 decibels. 10 is 10 decibels. That's a large drop, and the sender should adapt to a slower, more robust rate. Each station can react to its own radio conditions. But here's something it can't deal with alone. How do many stations share this one radio channel? Here's a very different answer to that question.

In a crowded room, two pairs can talk at once if one pair speaks English and the other speaks French. You filter out what you can't decode. Could two senders transmit on the same frequency at the same time, with the receiver still separating them?

That's the idea behind code division multiple access. Each sender gets its own code, a sequence of plus and minus ones, called chips. Sender one uses 1, 1, minus 1, minus 1. Sender two uses 1, minus 1, 1, minus 1. The magic is in how these two relate. Multiply them chip by chip, and add: 1, minus 1, minus 1, plus 1. That's zero. The codes are orthogonal.

To send a bit, multiply the whole code by the bit's value. Sender one sends plus 1, so it transmits its code unchanged. Sender two sends minus 1, so it transmits its code flipped. On the air, the signals simply add. Chip by chip, the receiver gets 0, 2, minus 2, 0. This sum looks like neither sender.

Decode. To hear sender one, take the dot product of the received signal with c 1, then divide by 4, the code length. 0 times 1, plus 2 times 1, plus minus 2 times minus 1, plus 0. That's 4, over 4, which is plus 1. Sender one's bit is recovered. With c 2, 0, minus 2, minus 2, plus 0 gives minus 4, over 4, which is minus 1. Why does this work? Correlating with c 1 leaves sender two's contribution multiplied by c 1 dot c 2, and that's zero. Sender two simply vanishes.

In formula form: the sum of each bit times its code goes out on the air. The receiver takes z dot c k, over M, the code length. This is an ideal model. It assumes synchronized chips and well balanced powers. It's a clean demonstration, not a promise of zero interference in the real world.
Don't treat orthogonality as magic. It cancels the other sender only under ideal conditions: synchronized chips, balanced powers, and little noise.
Change one bit. Sender one also sends minus 1, so both bits are minus 1.
What's the new sum z? And what do you get when you decode each sender?

z is minus 2, 0, 0, 2. Correlate with c 1: minus 2, plus 0, minus 0, minus 2, which is minus 4, over 4, or minus 1. Correlate with c 2: also minus 4 over 4, or minus 1. Both bits come out right. Codes are one way to share a medium, and cellular networks have used them. But Wi-Fi takes a completely different approach. Before that, a laptop has to find a network to join in the first place.

Open your laptop in a coffee shop. Several networks appear, and you click one. What has actually happened? Are you on the Internet yet? And when the frame leaves the laptop, whose address goes on it, the access point's, or the router's?

Start with the vocabulary. An access point and the stations associated with it form a basic service set, or BSS. Wi-Fi divides its spectrum into channels, and each access point operates on a chosen channel. Neighboring access points on overlapping channels interfere. The SSID is the human-readable network name, and the BSSID identifies one particular BSS. None of these are subnet masks, or IP addresses.

How do you find one? Two ways. In passive scanning, access points regularly send out beacons, and the laptop just listens. In active scanning, the laptop sends a probe request, and access points answer with probe responses. Either way, you end up with a list of candidates, and you choose one. Passive scanning costs the laptop only listening time. Active scanning finds networks sooner, at the price of a few transmissions.

That final exchange, a request and a reply, is association. It creates a link-layer relationship with one access point. It doesn't give you an IP address. So your laptop still needs DHCP, then ARP, then DNS, exactly as in chapter 5. Being associated means you can reach the AP, and nothing more.

The frame. An access point isn't a router. It bridges between radio and Ethernet. So a Wi-Fi frame needs to name both the immediate radio hop, and the final link-layer destination. Say host H1 sends to router R. Address one is the receiver on this radio hop, the AP. Address two is the transmitter, H1. Address three is R's MAC, which is where the AP should bridge the frame. The AP then emits an ordinary Ethernet frame, from H1 to R. H1 stays the Ethernet source. The AP never becomes the IP destination.

There's also a fourth address field. The slide says address 4 appears only in ad hoc mode, but its own table shows a bridged case. Don't memorize that note as a universal rule. Four-address operation is used for bridging and distribution scenarios.

Move. The laptop walks from access point 1 to access point 2. Both connect to one switch, on the same subnet. It associates with AP 2. Its IP address stays valid, because the subnet hasn't changed. So who updates what? The switch does, through its ordinary self-learning. The laptop's next frame arrives on a new port, so the switch's table changes. No Internet routes change. Chapter 2's mechanism handles this mobility case for free.
Keep the steps apart. Scanning finds an AP, and association attaches to it. Neither one gives you an IP address. That's still DHCP's job, afterward.
Change the scenario. A new access point has the very same SSID, but it sits behind a different router, on a different IP subnet.
Does the laptop keep working with its old address? Does matching SSID text guarantee anything?

It does not keep working. The old address doesn't belong on that subnet, so return traffic gets routed to the wrong place. A matching SSID is just a matching name. What counts is subnet continuity. Crossing subnets is the true mobility problem, and we'll take that on next chapter. First, a problem that hits every Wi-Fi network: when stations share one channel, who's allowed to talk?

Ethernet senders listen before and during transmission, and they abort on a collision. Why can't Wi-Fi do the same thing? It has a radio, it can listen. Is there something about radio that breaks collision detection?

There are two reasons. First, while transmitting, a radio's own signal overwhelms the tiny signal arriving from elsewhere, so it can't really listen while it talks. Second, and more deeply, what matters isn't what the sender hears. What matters is what the receiver hears. That difference needs a picture.

A, B, and C sit in a row. Each one's radio range reaches only its neighbors. A hears B. C hears B. But A and C can't hear each other. A senses the channel: silence. It starts sending to B. C senses too: silence, because it's out of A's range. It also starts sending to B. Each sender was perfectly polite, and both frames are destroyed at B. Neither of them noticed anything. This is the hidden terminal problem. Local sensing simply can't see interference at a distant receiver.

There's a mirror image. Now B sends to A, and C wants to send to D, on the far side. C hears B, so carrier sense says wait. But C's signal wouldn't reach A at all. These two transmissions could have happened at the same time safely. Sensing suppressed useful concurrency. That's the exposed terminal problem. A note of care, though. The slide's shortcut, about hearing an RTS but not a CTS, is an idealized thought experiment. Real timing and acknowledgments must work too, so the drawing alone isn't permission to transmit.

Wi-Fi avoids collisions instead of detecting them. It's called CSMA/CA. Here's the sender's routine. Wait until the channel has been idle for a period called DIFS. Then count down a random backoff, one idle slot at a time. If the channel goes busy, freeze the counter. Do not reset it. Transmit when it reaches zero. Then the receiver checks the frame, and after a shorter gap called SIFS, returns an ACK. Why shorter? So the ACK goes first, before anyone else can grab the channel. If no ACK arrives, the sender retries with a larger backoff range.

Trace a counter. It starts at 4. Two idle slots go by, and it reads 2. Another station transmits for a long time, and the counter stays at 2. When the channel is idle again, two more slots bring it to zero, and we can send. The waiting already done is not thrown away, which makes things fairer for stations that have waited.

And a missing ACK does not prove a collision. The data might have been corrupted by noise, or the ACK itself might have been lost. Note too that this is a local, link-layer ACK, not TCP's. It repairs one radio hop. Together with coding, retries, and rate changes, that's wireless error recovery. It's done locally because the radio hop is where the errors happen. Local repair doesn't guarantee end to end delivery, though.

CSMA/CA still doesn't cure the hidden terminal. For that, there's an optional reservation. Before sending data, A sends a short request to send, RTS, to B. B answers with clear to send, CTS. Here's the clever part. CTS comes from the receiver, so everybody near the receiver hears it, including hidden C. Now C knows to stay quiet. Then A sends the data, and B acknowledges.

How long should C stay quiet? The CTS carries a duration, and C sets a timer, called the network allocation vector, or NAV. This acts as virtual carrier sensing. Even during silent gaps between the protected frames, C treats the channel as busy.

Is this free? No. RTS frames can themselves collide, but they're short, so a collision costs much less than losing a long data frame. And the four-frame exchange adds overhead. For short frames on a quiet channel, that overhead can exceed what it saves. So choose it for long frames under real contention.

Radio also costs battery, and listening is expensive. In power management, a station tells its AP it's going to sleep. The AP buffers any frames for it. Each beacon lists who has data waiting. So the station wakes just in time for the beacon, and if it's named, it asks for its frames. Otherwise it goes straight back to sleep.

Notice the shared pattern with soft state and with queues. The AP holds data on the sleeper's behalf, and a periodic signal tells it when to check. You pay with delay, and you gain battery. There's a tradeoff in every design here.

Bluetooth shows yet another coordination model. A piconet has one controller, which schedules its nearby devices, so there's no contention at all. It also uses frequency hopping, moving among channels in a pattern. The slide's classic figures are 79 channels, and a 625 microsecond slot. Those describe the classic system, not all Bluetooth modes.

With 625 microseconds per slot, 1,600 slots fit in one second. The controller grants one client a transmit opportunity at a time, and the group follows a shared hopping sequence. These are classic Bluetooth's numbers, so don't apply them to every mode.
A hidden terminal isn't simply a weak signal. The key is two senders that can't hear each other, while both reach a shared receiver.
Test yourself on the geometry. A sends RTS to B. B's CTS is heard by C, which can't hear A. Separately, E can hear A, but not B.
Which station sets its NAV from the CTS? Which station hears only the RTS? And what might each one do?

C hears the CTS, so it sets its NAV, and it defers. That protects B's reception. E hears only the RTS. RTS frames also carry a duration, so in the standard behavior, E sets its NAV too, even though it might not harm B. E is exposed, and the shortcut of ignoring it is the idealization we flagged. So the radio link now works, for a laptop that stays put. But what if it doesn't? When a phone drives across a city, changing towers every few minutes, how can a call stay up, and how can anyone even find it?

Our laptop has become a phone, and now it's moving at highway speed, while it streams video. Its local Wi-Fi tricks are no help at this scale. A cellular carrier must find the phone anywhere in the country, keep its session alive across towers, and bill the right person. What kind of network can do all this?

Follow the history, since it explains the design. 2G was built for voice, like the telephone network. A radio site, called a BTS, connects to a base station controller, a BSC. Those connect to a mobile switching center, the MSC, and a gateway leads to the public telephone network. It's circuit switched throughout.

3G had to add data, without breaking voice. So it built a parallel packet core. The SGSN and GGSN form a data path to the Internet, sitting right beside the unchanged voice path. Voice and data share the radio side, and split at the edge of the core. That's the key insight: coexistence, not replacement.
Watch one handset use both. Its voice call follows the MSC side. Its packet data follows the SGSN and GGSN side, toward the Internet.

4G LTE makes a clean break. Everything, even voice, is carried as IP packets through one all-IP core. There's no separate circuit side. But all-IP doesn't mean ordinary routers and nothing else. LTE keeps specialized machinery for subscribers, authentication, location, radio scheduling, and tunnels.

Let's assign each piece one main role. The UE, or user element, is the device, along with its subscription. The subscription is identified by an IMSI. This is an identity that stays the same, not a location. The slide calls it 64 bit, and draws it like a MAC address. In the standard, it's a string of no more than 15 decimal digits. The point to keep is that it's separate from any MAC, IP, or tunnel address.
The eNodeB is the base station. It's not a passive relay. It manages radio resources, and takes an active part in attachment and handover. It's where the wireless hop meets the core.

For example, base station A decides that a target, B, should serve a moving phone. It asks B for resources, and later directs the phone there. The core's tunnel state then moves to match. An ordinary Ethernet switch does nothing like this.

The home subscriber server, the HSS, lives in the subscriber's home network. It stores who you are and what you're allowed to do, and it cooperates in authentication. It isn't on the path of your data at all.

Picture a phone appearing in a visited network. Its mobility manager coordinates with the home HSS, to authenticate the subscription and set up state for the visit. That's a database and control role. No user packet ever passes through it.

The mobility management entity, the MME, is the coordinator. It handles authentication with the HSS, tracks where the device is, handles paging, and sets up the tunnels. It tells other boxes what to do, but user data doesn't pass through it.

The serving gateway and the packet gateway are on the user's data path. The P-GW connects to external networks, such as the Internet. The S-GW joins the radio-side tunnel to the tunnel toward the P-GW. To see the point, watch a packet. It goes UE, eNodeB, S-GW, P-GW. It never touches the MME or the HSS.

The P-GW is the cellular system's outward doorway. The radio cell can change, while traffic stays anchored through that gateway. It may also perform NAT. But NAT translation and tunnel encapsulation are different operations, so don't treat them as one.

Draw two separate pictures. The control story has the HSS and the MME. The payload story has the S-GW and the P-GW. A control message can change a data path without its sender being one of the hops. That's the data plane and control plane split again, from chapter 3.
A tempting error is to route user data through every box in the diagram. The HSS and MME do control work. Payload travels through the base station, the S-GW, and the P-GW.
Test that. Suppose the MME crashes for a moment, while a phone is sitting still, in the middle of a video stream. Separately, suppose the S-GW crashes.
Which failure immediately stops the video's packets? And which one affects moving phones, and new ones?

An S-GW failure stops the packets right away, since it's on the data path. The tunnels that are already set up don't pass through the MME, so its failure hits control tasks first, like attaching, paging, and handover. So, the data flows through a chain of tunnels. What's inside those tunnels, and how does the radio hop actually work? That's next.

A phone's IP packet has to cross a noisy radio link, then a carrier's core network, and every few minutes the radio end of that path moves. How do you carry a packet through all that, so the packet itself never needs to know?

Start with the radio hop. LTE splits its link layer into pieces. PDCP handles header compression and encryption, so scarce radio bits aren't wasted on bulky headers. RLC handles fragmentation and reassembly, and reliable transfer over the radio. Below that sits the medium access layer. Note that RLC segmentation is not IPv4 fragmentation. The headers are different, and so is the scope of reassembly. The radio link fixes its own problems locally.

How do users share the radio? Unlike Wi-Fi, there's no contention for the downlink. The base station is a scheduler. It uses OFDM, which divides the channel into many orthogonal frequency subcarriers. Picture a grid, with time along one axis, and frequency along the other. The scheduler hands each small block to one user. A user with good conditions may get more. That grid only shows opportunities, and doesn't give you application throughput, because coding, modulation, and overhead still apply.

The core. Inside the core, the phone's packet isn't routed by its own address. It travels in a tunnel, using GTP, the GPRS tunneling protocol. The eNodeB wraps the phone's IP packet in a GTP header, that in UDP, and that in an outer IP header addressed to the S-GW. Core routers read only that outer header. The S-GW then unwraps and rewraps, into a new tunnel toward the P-GW. There the outer layers come off, and the original packet heads into the Internet, unchanged.

What's the benefit of all that wrapping? The radio end of the tunnel can change, without every Internet router learning a new route for this phone. The inner address stays fixed, while only the outer destination moves. And the core needs nothing beyond plain IP routing.

How does a phone get started? It first synchronizes with a nearby cell, and reads broadcast system information. It selects a base station. Then control setup, with authentication through the MME and HSS. And finally the data path is built. Finding a signal doesn't prove that a tunnel, or even an authorized subscription, is ready. Those are distinct stages.

Radios drain batteries, so an idle phone sleeps. It can go into a deeper sleep, where it no longer tracks a specific cell, and then the network knows it only roughly. To reach it, the network pages it across that area. When it wakes, it might have moved, and may need a new association. It's the same trade-off as Wi-Fi sleep: battery against delivery, with cellular machinery.

Follow one phone. It sleeps, moves into another cell, and then becomes active. The old radio path can't simply be assumed, so it may need to reestablish access through the new cell before traffic can resume.

One more view. Carriers are networks of IP networks, joined by interconnections, just like the rest of the Internet. Your phone might attach in a visited network, while your subscriber record stays at home, in your home carrier's HSS. So every topic in this course reappears here: tunnels, routers, and policy agreements between providers.

5G New Radio extends the physical layer. Higher frequencies offer more capacity, but shorter range, so cells must be much denser. MIMO uses many antennas to send and receive multiple spatial streams. The slide's specific rates and goals describe the era of those slides, so treat them as context. The trade-off is what lasts: more spectrum and antennas for capacity, paid for with deployment density.
Don't mix these up. CDMA separates senders by code. OFDM organizes the channel by frequency and time, and the scheduler hands out those resources.
Look at one packet, deep in the core, between S-GW and P-GW. Its inner destination is a web server on the Internet.
Which address does a core router in the middle use to forward it? Does that router need a route to the phone?

It reads the outer destination, the P-GW. It needs no route to the phone at all. That's the whole benefit: a carrier's core routers know nothing about individual subscribers. And now the big question. Your phone has moved between cities, or even to another carrier's network. Its identity hasn't changed, but where it sits has. How does anybody find it?

The problem that was planted back in chapter 3. An IP address says where you are in the topology. That's what makes routing scale. So what happens when you move? Your old address now points to the wrong place. But your identity, the thing others use to contact you, hasn't changed. One number has been doing two jobs.

One approach: let the routing system handle it. Have the phone advertise its own slash 32 from wherever it is. Routers would find it, in principle. But think about billions of devices, each changing location constantly, with each change spreading through every router in the world. That would be enormous, rapidly changing routing state. And it would destroy the very aggregation that makes routing scale. So we push the problem to the edge instead.

Split the two roles. The home network is the provider you subscribe to. It always knows who you are. The visited network is wherever you currently are. It provides access, and tells your home where you've gone. This happens even between countries. In cellular, the HSS is on the home side. The generic Mobile IP example and LTE share this principle, even though the protocols and components have different names.

A constructed Mobile IP example. The mobile's home address is 192.0.2.20. On arriving at a visited network, it gets a current locator, called a care-of address, 198.51.100.44. It registers this with its home agent, which records a binding from home address to care-of address. The drawing has a foreign agent ending the tunnel. A co-located care-of address, where the mobile itself ends the tunnel, is another valid arrangement. And don't mix this generic Mobile IP up with LTE's HSS, MME, and GTP.

A correspondent sends to the mobile. It uses the home address, not knowing anything has changed. The packet arrives at the home network. The home agent intercepts it, and puts the whole packet inside a new one: an outer IP header, from the home agent to the care-of address. That's IP tunneling. Routers in the middle follow only the outer header. At the far end, the outer header comes off, and out comes the original packet, with its source and destination unchanged. This is indirect routing. The correspondent never needed to know about the move.

Tunnels cost bytes. An illustrative outer IPv4 header adds 20 bytes. A 1,480 byte inner packet becomes 1,500, which just fits an Ethernet link. A 1,500 byte inner packet becomes 1,520, and that needs different MTU treatment. And don't confuse tunneling with NAT. NAT rewrites addresses. A tunnel adds an envelope.

Watch the mobile move again, to a new locator, 203.0.113.44. It re-registers. The home agent updates its binding. The outer destination changes. The inner destination stays right where it was. That's the visual to hold on to: identity in blue, unchanged, and location in the outer header, changing.

What's the downside of indirect delivery? A detour. Traffic goes through the home agent, even when the correspondent is right next to the mobile. This is triangle routing. In this constructed example, the correspondent to home agent takes 40 milliseconds. Then 50 more to the mobile. That's 90, while a direct path would only take 10. It's a detour, not a loop.

Direct routing removes the detour. The correspondent obtains the current locator, then tunnels straight to it. It saves 80 milliseconds here. But the price is complexity. The correspondent must now handle bindings. And when the mobile moves again, something must handle packets aimed at the old location. Neither design removes location state. It only changes who holds and uses it.
When you trace a tunnel, always say which header you mean. The outer destination changes. The inner source and destination don't. An answer that just says, the destination, is ambiguous.
Change the geography. Correspondent to home agent is 60 milliseconds. Home agent to mobile is 70. Direct is 5.
What's the one-way delay with each design? And if the correspondent is actually beside the home agent, does the triangle still hurt?

Indirect is 130 milliseconds, and direct is 5. But if the home agent is near the path anyway, the detour shrinks to nothing. It depends on geometry. Now one piece remains. All of this assumed a phone that has already arrived somewhere. What about the moment of moving itself, in the middle of a video, from one tower to another?

A phone at highway speed leaves one cell, and enters the next, in the middle of a stream. The radio link must move. The tunnel must move. Packets are already in flight toward the old tower. How can you change all of this without dropping the session?

This is handover. Here's the setup. Packets come from the S-GW through a tunnel to base station A, then over the radio to the phone. Base station B sits next door, and it's stronger as the phone drives toward it. Base station A notices this from the phone's radio reports.

Step one. A chooses B as the target, and asks it to get ready. Step two. B reserves radio resources, and acknowledges. Nothing has moved yet, and the phone keeps working as before. Prepare first, and then act, so that the target is ready when the phone arrives.

Step three. A tells the phone to switch, and the phone begins using B. The radio has moved. But the S-GW has not been told, and it's still sending to A. So what happens to those packets? Step four. A forwards them to B, over a temporary path. So during this period, the path is S-GW, A, B, phone. It's longer, but nothing's lost.

Step five. B reports that the move is complete. The MME tells the S-GW to change its tunnel endpoint from A to B. See that this is a control message, and the MME isn't carrying any data. Step six. The S-GW now sends straight to B, and A releases its old resources. The outer destination changed. The inner packet, and the phone's IP address, did not.
There are three paths to remember. Before: S-GW, A, phone. During: S-GW, A, B, phone. After: S-GW, B, phone. The middle stage explains how the radio can finish moving before the core catches up.

Does a preserved IP address mean nothing changes for TCP? No. The longer forwarding path raises delay for a while. Packets can arrive out of order. Radio errors and local retries make round trip times swing around. IP is still best effort, and its contract hasn't changed. But TCP might read these effects as congestion, even when no queue is full. The details of transport belong to later lectures. For now, keep the link: what lower layers do can change the performance higher layers see.
During handover, notice who carries what. The MME only sends control messages. The data goes from the S-GW, through A, and on to B.
Change the order. Imagine a design where the S-GW switches its tunnel to B first, before the phone has actually moved.
What happens to packets for those moments? And is there any forwarding path that would save them?

Packets reach B, but the phone is still attached to A, so B has nobody to give them to. They would need buffering, or they'd be lost. The real ordering avoids this: the radio moves first, and packets follow, by way of A, and only then does the core switch. Order matters, just as it did with routing convergence. And with that, every piece of the story is in place. So let's put it all together, one last time.

We began with one question. How does a packet reach the right place, when no device knows the whole path? Now we can answer it. Every mechanism in this course supplies one missing fact, keeps some state, picks one action, or contains one failure. Let's retell the entire journey, and then test it on problems that cross chapters.

A laptop wakes up. Wi-Fi association attaches it to an access point, and a broadcast to DHCP gives it an address, mask, gateway, and resolver. Its mask says the resolver is remote, so ARP finds the gateway's MAC address. A frame carries the DNS query to R1. The resolver walks the hierarchy, using caches when it can, and returns an A record. Now the laptop can send to the server.

The frame crosses switches, which learned their tables from source addresses. At R1 the frame is replaced, while the packet's endpoints stay fixed, and TTL drops by one. Longest prefix match selects the output. The packet crosses the fabric, waits in a queue, and leaves. Those tables came from the control plane: link state or distance vector inside an AS, and BGP between ASes, shaped by contracts, with the next hop resolved through internal routing.

When something breaks, detection, propagation, computation, and installation all take time, and in between come blackholes and loops. If the destination is a group, IGMP learns local interest, and PIM connects the routers. If it's one of many, routing picks an instance. And when the receiver moves, a tunnel carries the same inner packet to a changing outer destination, while control messages move the endpoints. The envelope is local, and the packet is global. At each layer, the question is who knows what.
Before the problems, one last trap. Exam answers go wrong when mechanisms blur together. Each one supplies one missing fact. Name the fact first, and then the mechanism.
Mixed problems. Problem one. A host at 10.10.1.97/23 sends to 10.10.0.200. Then to 10.10.2.5. Its gateway is 10.10.0.1. Which IP address does it ARP for, each time? Think in terms of the mask.

The block covers third byte values 0 and 1. So 10.10.0.200 is local, and the host ARPs for 10.10.0.200 itself. 10.10.2.5 is outside the block, so it ARPs for its gateway, 10.10.0.1. The mask decides, not how the numbers look.

Problem two. A router uses distance vector. Its link to neighbor A costs 2, and A says 7. Its link to neighbor B costs 5, and B says 1. Which route wins? Then the destination fails, and B had been routing through this very router. What goes wrong, and which fix applies?

Through A costs 9, and through B costs 6, so B wins. But wait. If B reaches the destination through this router, then B's advertised 1 could be stale, with no real path behind it. The result is count to infinity, on a two-node dependency. Poison reverse would have had B advertise infinity back to us, so that the false route would never have been considered at all.

Problem three. Your AS has a route from a provider with local preference 80 and an AS path of length 2, and a route from a customer with local preference 100 and length 5. You pick one. Which do you use? And would you advertise the other to your peer?

You use the customer route, because preference comes first, so path length never comes into it here. You'd advertise that customer route to your peer, since customer routes go everywhere. The provider route you would not offer to a peer, even if it were your only route, because that would make you carry traffic between two non-customers.

Problem four. A 2,000 byte datagram, with a 20 byte header, must cross a link with an MTU of 1,500. Which bytes go in the first fragment? What offset does the second one carry? Then its destination, 201.10.6.200, meets the same three-entry table as before. Which output?

The data is 1,980 bytes. The first fragment carries 1,480, at offset 0, with the more fragments flag set. The second carries 500, at offset 185, with the flag cleared. For lookup, 201.10.6.200 matches the slash 21, the slash 23, and the slash 0, so the slash 23 wins: output B. Each fragment gets the same lookup, since every fragment has the same destination.

Problem five. A multicast router reaches source S through port 2. A packet from S to group G arrives on port 4, and later on port 2. Its LAN has one member, and that member sends a leave. What happens at each step?

On port 4, the reverse path test fails, so it's dropped as a likely duplicate. On port 2, it passes, and the packet is forwarded onto interested outputs. When the member leaves, the router doesn't prune right away. It sends a group-specific query, since others might remain. When no one answers, it stops forwarding there, and if no other branches want the data, it prunes upstream. IGMP handled the LAN, and PIM handled the routers.

Last one. A phone's tunnel runs through S-GW to base station A, and a correspondent reaches the phone's stable address. The phone hands over to base station B. Which fields change in the packet that the S-GW sends afterward?
Name exactly what changes, and what stays the same.

The outer destination changes, from A to B. The inner packet stays the same. That's the picture you started this course with, one final time. The blue address persists, while an outer envelope changes around it. At the very beginning it was yellow, on one Ethernet link. Now it's a tunnel across a cellular core. It's the same idea at a new scale. When you face a new mechanism, ask what's missing, who knows it, what state is kept, and what happens when that state goes stale. If you can trace one packet through it with real addresses, you understand it. Next, try the practice midterm walkthrough in chapter 13, and use the study player to answer before each explanation.

Practice question 1. This walkthrough follows a generated practice midterm, not your instructor's exam, so use it to test your reasoning, not to predict questions. If you haven't tried the test yet, stop now and take it first. A switch starts with an empty table. A is on port 1, B is on port 2, and C is on port 3, all in one VLAN. Trace A to B, then B to A, then C to B. After each frame, give the table change and the output ports.
Work all three frames before going on.
First frame, A to B. The switch reads the source address, so it learns that A is on port 1. Then it looks up the destination. B is unknown, so it floods out ports 2 and 3.
Second frame, B to A. Source first: B is on port 2. Now the destination, A, is in the table, so the frame goes only out port 1.
Third frame, C to B. The source teaches the switch that C is on port 3. B is known, so the frame goes out port 2. The final table is A on 1, B on 2, and C on 3.

The tempting mistake. After the first frame, many people write B into the table, because A mentioned B. But a destination address tells the switch nothing about where B is. Only a frame sent by B can do that.
On marks: three points for the three forwarding actions, and two for source learning with the correct final table.
